profile.summary: gLM2 is a genomic language model that reads a stretch of genome as a mixture of two alphabets: protein coding regions as amino acids, and the intergenic sequence between them as nucleotides. Each element is prefixed with a strand token. It is a transformer encoder trained by masked language modelling on the OMG metagenomic corpus, and the authors say its representations carry functional information as well as coevolutionary signals in protein-protein interfaces and genomic regulatory syntax.
profile.summary_source_locator: README.md: Model Description; model card: Model Description; Europe PMC abstract

sections.title: How it works
sections.body: gLM2 is a transformer encoder trained with the masked language modelling objective: 30% of both amino-acid and nucleotide tokens are masked, and cross-entropy loss is applied only on the masked tokens. The input is a contig written as alternating coding and intergenic elements: coding elements as uppercase amino acids, intergenic elements as lowercase nucleotides, so the two alphabets cannot collide, and each element prefixed by <+> or <-> for the strand. The paper's motivation is that nucleotide-only models need very long contexts for genes, while protein-only genomic models ignore the regulatory sequence between genes. The 650M checkpoint has depth 33, dimension 1280 and 20 heads; the 150M checkpoint has depth 30, dimension 640 and 10 heads; both use RoPE, SwiGLU and RMS normalisation. Both were trained for 600k steps, 315B tokens, with a context length of 4096. An update in September 2024 raised the context from 2048 to 4096 tokens and changed intergenic tokenisation from BPE to per-nucleotide.

Both cards carry the same September 2024 update note, the same 315B pretraining tokens and the same 4096 context length, and their configs differ in size: depth 33 and dimension 1280 for 650M, depth 30 and dimension 640 for 150M. A result should name which checkpoint was used and its Hugging Face revision, because the September 2024 update changed both the context length and the intergenic tokenisation. strengths.text: The authors report that the categorical Jacobian of gLM2_650M on the concatenated ModA and ModC sequences (PDB 2ONK) shows inter-protein contacts that match an MSA-based coevolution model, checked against the PDB structure, where they say ESM2 650M and Evo show none.

limitations.text: Input must be prepared, not raw DNA: coding regions have to be called and translated to uppercase amino acids, intergenic sequence kept as lowercase nucleotides, and each element given a strand token. The tokenizer depends on that case and on the strand tokens.

The context is 4096 tokens, so only a short stretch of a genome fits in one pass. The September 2024 update raised it from 2048 tokens and changed the intergenic tokenisation, so the checkpoint revision matters when reporting a result.

The training corpus is metagenomic and, in the paper's words, primarily prokaryotic and viral. The paper says common gene-calling tools fail on eukaryotic sequences and that the corpus uses the databases' own gene predictions, so protein sequences predicted from eukaryotic contigs may be of poor quality.
The published usage example calls .cuda() and loads custom model code with trust_remote_code, so a CUDA GPU is assumed and remote code is executed.

run_guide.summary: Load the gLM2 650M checkpoint and extract embeddings for a short mixed-modality contig.
prerequisites: Python with PyTorch and transformers.
A CUDA GPU: the published example calls .cuda() and loads the weights in bfloat16. Memory needs are not stated in the sources read.
Code and weights are Apache-2.0 and the checkpoints are not gated.
The input must already be split into coding and intergenic elements, with amino acids uppercase and nucleotides lowercase.

steps.explanation: The sources name no install command; this line installs the two packages their usage example imports.

steps.title: Extract embeddings for a contig
steps.shell:
python - <<'PY'
import torch
from transformers import AutoModel, AutoTokenizer

model = AutoModel.from_pretrained('tattabio/gLM2_650M', torch_dtype=torch.bfloat16, trust_remote_code=True).cuda()
tokenizer = AutoTokenizer.from_pretrained('tattabio/gLM2_650M', trust_remote_code=True)

# A contig with two proteins and an inter-genic sequence.
# NOTE: Nucleotides should always be lowercase, and prepended with `<+>`.
sequence = "<+>MALTKVEKRNRIKRRVRGKISGTQASPRLSVYKSNK<+>aatttaaggaa<->MLGIDNIERVKPGGLELVDRLVAVNRVTKVTKGGRAFGFSAIVVVGNED"

# Tokenize the sequence.
encodings = tokenizer([sequence], return_tensors='pt')

# Extract embeddings.
with torch.no_grad():
    embeddings = model(encodings.input_ids.cuda(), output_hidden_states=True).last_hidden_state
PY
steps.explanation: The model card's example, wrapped in a shell heredoc. For the smaller model use tattabio/gLM2_150M, as the card and README name it.

profile.summary: RNAErnie is an RNA language model that turns an RNA sequence into embeddings for downstream prediction. During pretraining it uses known RNA motifs as prior knowledge and masks them at random, alongside the usual masked language modelling. Its developers fine-tune it for RNA sequence classification, RNA-RNA interaction prediction and RNA secondary structure prediction.
profile.summary_source_locator: README.md: opening paragraphs

sections.title: How it works
sections.body: The original RNAErnie is a 12-layer ERNIE transformer with hidden size 768, written in PaddlePaddle. It is pretrained on about 23 million RNAcentral ncRNA sequences of up to 512 nucleotides with three masking levels, chosen at random in a 1:1:1 ratio: base-level masking of 15% of nucleotides, masking of contiguous subsequences of 4 to 8 bases, and motif-level masking of motifs gathered from ATtRACT, SpliceAid and the most frequent 4 to 8 base sequences in RNAcentral. An [IND] token followed by the sequence's RNA type is appended during pretraining. For downstream tasks the paper offers a frozen backbone with a trainable head (FBTH), a trainable backbone and head (TBTH), and a two-stage type-guided STACK design that first predicts the top-K RNA types, appends each to the sequence and averages the K predictions weighted by their probabilities. For secondary structure prediction it computes four folding scores per base pair and decodes with Zuker-style dynamic programming, using a module compiled from mxfold2. Pretraining ran about 2,580,000 steps with batch size 50 on four Nvidia Tesla V100 32 GB GPUs for around 250 hours. The authors' later PyTorch checkpoint is a separate BERT masked language model with 12 layers, hidden size 768, 12 attention heads and an 11-token vocabulary.
sections.source_locator: README.md; config.json; paper: Methods (RNAErnie transformer, Motif-aware pretraining strategies, Type-guided fine-tuning strategy, Hyperparameters and configurations)

sections.title: Versions and reproducibility
sections.body: There are two lines of checkpoints. The original PaddlePaddle model from the paper, with masking-strategy variants and task-specific fine-tuned weights, is distributed through Google Drive folders linked from the README; an ad-hoc variant pretrained with an extra classification loss and a 1-epoch checkpoint are also linked. In June 2024 the developers trained a separate PyTorch model from scratch with a maximum length of 2048 on a newer RNAcentral release of about 31 million sequences, and published it on Hugging Face (now LLM-EDA/RNAErnie); its tokenisation differs slightly from the original. A result should say which of these checkpoints was used.

steps.title: Extract embeddings
steps.shell:
python - <<'PY'
import paddle
from rna_ernie import BatchConverter
from paddlenlp.transformers import ErnieModel

# ========== Set device
paddle.set_device("gpu")

# ========== Prepare Data
data = [
    ("RNA1", "GGGUGCGAUCAUACCAGCACUAAUGCCCUCCUGGGAAGUCCUCGUGUUGCACCCCU"),
    ("RNA2", "GGGUGUCGCUCAGUUGGUAGAGUGCUUGCCUGGCAUGCAAGAAACCUUGGUUCAAUCCCCAGCACUGCA"),
    ("RNA3", "CGAUUCNCGUUCCC--CCGCCUCCA"),
]

# ========== Batch Converter
batch_converter = BatchConverter(k_mer=1,
                                  vocab_path="./data/vocab/vocab_1MER.txt",
                                  batch_size=256,
                                  max_seq_len=512)

# ========== RNAErnie Model
rna_ernie = ErnieModel.from_pretrained("output/BERT,ERNIE,MOTIF,PROMPT/checkpoint_final/")
rna_ernie.eval()

# call batch_converter to convert sequences to batch inputs
for names, _, inputs_ids in batch_converter(data):
    with paddle.no_grad():
        # extract whole sequence embeddings
        embeddings = rna_ernie(inputs_ids)[0].detach()
        # extract [CLS] token embedding
        embeddings_cls = embeddings[:, 0, :]
        print(names, embeddings.shape, embeddings_cls.shape)
PY

profile.summary: UTR-LM is a language model for the 5' untranslated region (5' UTR) of mRNA, the stretch before the coding sequence that strongly affects how well an mRNA is translated. It reads a 5' UTR sequence and, after fine-tuning, predicts mean ribosome loading, translation efficiency or mRNA expression level. Pretraining combines masked language modelling with labels computed from the sequence, such as secondary structure and minimum free energy.
profile.summary_source_locator: README.md opening paragraph; bioRxiv abstract

sections.title: How it works
sections.body: UTR-LM is built on a modified copy of the ESM-2 transformer code, shipped in the repository. Each nucleotide is a token, a [CLS] token is added, and tokens become 128-dimensional vectors fed to six transformer layers with 16 attention heads. Pretraining masks 15% of nucleotides and reconstructs them (masked nucleotide task). Two optional supervised tasks use labels computed with ViennaRNA: predicting the secondary-structure symbol at masked positions, and predicting the minimum free energy (MFE) from the [CLS] representation with a two-layer feed-forward predictor. For downstream tasks the developers replace the MFE target with the task label and fine-tune the whole model, using a Huber loss in the README's commands. In the paper, the MRL model used the downstream library, secondary structure and MFE in pretraining, and the TE and EL models used the downstream library and MFE. Training ran on four V100-SXM2 16 GB GPUs on AWS and four P100 PCIe GPUs on a Stanford cluster, for at most 200 epochs and two days.

sections.body: The repository holds 16 pretrained checkpoint files under Model/Pretrained, named by their pretraining variant (ESM2, ESM2SI, ESM2SS, ESM2SISS, ESM2DSD) and data split, plus 179 checkpoint files under Model/Downstream: 178 for the TE and EL tasks and one for MRL (fold 0 of a single library). The README's own example pretraining command passes --heads 6 --embed_dim 16, which disagrees with the 16 heads and embedding size 128 listed under General Parameters and in the checkpoint file names. A result should name the exact checkpoint file and the repository commit. A runnable copy is also published as a CodeOcean capsule.

profile.summary: HyInv does inverse folding: given a protein backbone it proposes amino-acid sequences that should fold into it. The input is the N, C-alpha, C and O backbone atoms of a structure read from a PDB file; the output is a set of sequences, written as FASTA. It is a small graph network of 1,957,573 parameters that was trained first on natural and predicted structures and then by reinforcement learning against a structure predictor, and it ships as an installable Python package with its weights.
profile.summary_source_locator: README.md: opening paragraph, Usage, Layout; technical report Sections 2 and 2.1

sections.title: How it works
sections.body: HyInv follows the message-passing encoder and decoder design of ProteinMPNN. Each residue is joined to its 48 nearest neighbours and the edges carry distance features that do not change with rotation or translation. The encoder has 4 layers of width 128 and runs once for a backbone; the decoder has 3 layers of the same width and predicts amino-acid distributions at the masked positions from the backbone and the residues already visible. Training had two stages: supervision that maximised the likelihood of the native sequence under a random residue order, then reinforcement learning whose reward was mostly the scTM between the predicted structure of a candidate sequence and the input backbone. At inference the model needs no protein language model, no structure predictor and no alignment.
sections.source_locator: Technical report Sections 2.1, 2.2 and 2.3; README.md opening paragraph

sections.title: Sampling: draft and rewrite
sections.body: Sequences are not drawn in one pass. The positions are split at random into 8 fixed groups. A draft phase samples one group per round at temperature 0.6 starting from a fully masked sequence, and a rewrite phase then masks one group per round, keeps every other position visible, and resamples that group at temperature 0.34. Generating a design costs one encoder pass and 16 decoder passes. The authors report that separating the two temperatures gives a higher scTM at the same sequence diversity than sampling at a single temperature, by 0.0078 on CATH4.3 test and 0.0131 on RecentPDB, measured on an earlier checkpoint of the same run.
sections.source_locator: Technical report Sections 3.1 and 3.2; README.md opening paragraph

sections.title: Versions and reproducibility
sections.body: One checkpoint is released: the reinforcement-learning version, which the technical report identifies as update 640 with draft temperature 0.6 and rewrite temperature 0.34, the setting used for every result in the report. The supervised checkpoint that preceded it is described but not released. A result should name the setting as well as the checkpoint, because the package offers three numerical paths. The default reference path is FP32 and reproduces its own output for the same seed, batch size, device type and PyTorch version; the exact path is accelerated FP32 and almost always returns the same sequences; the bf16 path is a different arithmetic and does not return the same sequences for the same seed. Batch size is part of the seed, because batch k uses seed plus k, and the CPU and GPU random streams differ.
sections.source_locator: Technical report Sections 3.2 and 5.1, Table 1; README.md Notes and Accelerated inference

strengths.text: Small and cheap to run. The model has under two million parameters and runs on CPU as well as GPU, and the only required dependencies are PyTorch, safetensors and numpy.

strengths.text: Fast enough for library screening on one GPU: the authors measure 128 designs for a 402-residue backbone in 50.6 ms on an NVIDIA H20 with the bf16 path, and 10,000 designs for a 250-residue backbone in 2.11 s.
Needs nothing beyond the backbone at inference: no alignment, no protein language model and no structure predictor, and positions can be pinned so that a catalytic site or pocket is kept.

strengths.text: The developers report that on their five panels, with one panel scored by three structure predictors, HyInv reaches a higher average scTM than all ten external baselines at comparable or higher sequence diversity. This is the authors' own evaluation.

limitations.text: Single chains only in intent. The authors state that HyInv targets single-chain backbones and name multi-chain interfaces and membrane environments as future work, although the command line accepts several chains.

The fast bf16 path does not reproduce the reference sequences, so a result must say which path produced it. The exact path reproduces them almost always: in a check of about 8,000 sequences one differed at one position.

profile.summary: hEvo is a family of DNA language models from MulinLab trained on haplotype sequences from human populations, so that the models see real human genetic variation rather than one reference genome. A model reads a DNA sequence of up to 1,024 nucleotides and returns one vector per nucleotide, plus masked-base predictions that can score a single-nucleotide variant as a log-likelihood ratio of the alternative against the reference allele. The authors use it for variant-effect scoring, regulatory annotation and population-genetic analysis.
profile.summary_source_locator: README.md: Overview, Models; hEVO-base-o card: Model overview, Intended use

sections.title: How it works
sections.body: hEvo is a bidirectional BERT-style masked language model with one token per nucleotide, in two training stages. Stage I masked 20% of valid nucleotide positions in short contiguous spans and trained the encoder and prediction head together to recover them, with cross entropy computed only at masked positions. Stage II kept the encoder fixed and updated the whole masked-language-modelling head (its dense transformation, LayerNorm and nucleotide decoder) on contexts taken from an observed alternative-allele chromosome with the focal nucleotide masked, sampled equally across five alternative-allele frequency strata. Neither stage used clinical or functional labels. To score a single-nucleotide variant, the variant position is masked once and the log probability of the alternative allele minus that of the reference allele is taken from the same masked context; a positive value means the model prefers the alternative allele. The paper reports that this allelic refinement raised ClinVar AUPRC from 0.471 to 0.904 for its representative corpus with overlapping windows, without retraining the encoder.
sections.source_locator: README.md; model cards; paper: Results; Methods, Model architecture and sequence pretraining; Allelic refinement

sections.title: Versions and reproducibility
sections.body: The README lists primary models hEvo-base and hEvo-large, and public-data variants hEvo-open-base and hEvo-open-large, which are published on Hugging Face as hEVO-base-o (87.1M parameters, 12 layers, hidden size 768) and hEVO-large-o (319.5M parameters, 16 layers, hidden size 1,280). Only the two -o checkpoints are linked for download, and both are gated. The -o models were pretrained separately on public 1000 Genomes Project and HGDP data. The README says hEVO-base-o matches the hEvo-open-base weights by file hash, and that hEVO-large-o has identical tensors to the hEvo-open-large checkpoint after conversion. The model cards pin a code and weights revision in their examples (fa613904 for base, 09541834 for large) and keep the card itself on main. A result should name the checkpoint and that revision.
sections.source_locator: README.md: Models; hEVO-base-o and hEVO-large-o cards: Configuration at a glance, Checkpoint family, Load once

sections.title: What is public
sections.body: The public GitHub repository holds benchmark evaluators, numerical result tables and figure renderers, not the model code. The pretraining and cohort-preprocessing code sits in a separate Hugging Face repository that is also gated. That repository holds code and placeholder configurations only, without source data, generated training datasets or checkpoints.

facts.label: Model type
facts.value: DNA foundation model (masked nucleotide language model) trained on human population haplotypes.
facts.source_locator: README.md: title; hEVO-base-o card: Model overview

facts.label: Architecture
facts.value: Bidirectional transformer with nucleotide-level masked language modelling, one token per nucleotide. The paper's base configuration has 12 transformer blocks with 768-dimensional hidden states and the large configuration 16 blocks with 1,280-dimensional states, about 87 and 319 million parameters; the public checkpoints hEVO-base-o and hEVO-large-o match those two configurations. The sequence encoder feeds a prediction head of a dense transformation, GELU activation, LayerNorm and an untied vocabulary decoder. An optional frequency-embedding branch is disabled by default.
facts.source_locator: model cards: Configuration at a glance; paper: Methods, Model architecture and sequence pretraining

facts.label: Inputs
facts.value: A DNA string of 1 to 1,024 characters from A, C, G, T and N. Longer sequences must be split into windows by the user.
facts.source_locator: hEVO-base-o card: Load once, Input and output

facts.label: Outputs
facts.value: One hidden vector per nucleotide from the final layer; masked-LM logits over a 10-token vocabulary at each position; from these, an ALT-minus-REF log-likelihood ratio for a single-nucleotide variant. The card says the LLR is a model preference, not a calibrated probability of pathogenicity.

strengths.text: The developers report that hEvo-base or hEvo-large led the external models they judged eligible in 18 of 19 primary comparisons across functional annotation, variant interpretation and human evolution, with 87 million or 319 million parameters against billion-parameter comparators. This is the authors' own evaluation; the paper also records 5.93 and 14.86 ms per sequence for embedding extraction by base and large against 239.10 ms for Evo2-7B, and peak GPU allocations of 631 and 1,251 MiB against 5,491 MiB, in their own workloads.

limitations.text: Short context of about 1 kb (1,024 nucleotides); longer regions must be windowed, and the paper says this limits distal regulation and extended-haplotype modelling. Learning from population variants was restricted to single-nucleotide variants: indels and more complex structural variants were not modelled, and the variant score covers single-nucleotide changes only.
Loading runs Python code from the model repository (trust_remote_code), which the card asks users to review first.

The authors' own caveats on their results: held-out task labels do not exclude pretraining exposure to related sequences or individuals, so the population and retrospective clinical analyses are not tests of unseen populations or of prospective clinical use, and they say the absence of independent clinical validation limits deployment claims. The paper reports that hEVO-large-o was weaker than hEVO-large on unmarked regulatory element discrimination, association-based variant prioritisation and chromatin prediction, and that the public-resource models retain useful capabilities without reproducing every benefit of the larger corpus.

steps.title: Load the model and embed a sequence
steps.shell:
python - <<'EOF'
import torch
from transformers import AutoConfig, AutoModelForMaskedLM, AutoTokenizer

REPO = "MulinLab/hEVO-base-o"
# Freeze the checkpoint and its custom code for reproducible inference.
REVISION = "fa6139047c21d92b58bd8eda49ea2f89a884e33c"
device = torch.device("cuda" if torch.cuda.is_available() else "cpu")

load_options = dict(revision=REVISION, token=True, trust_remote_code=True)
tokenizer = AutoTokenizer.from_pretrained(REPO, **load_options)
config = AutoConfig.from_pretrained(
    REPO,
    use_frequency_embedding=False,
    use_flash_attention=False,
    **load_options,
)
assert config.use_frequency_embedding is False
model = AutoModelForMaskedLM.from_pretrained(
    REPO,
    config=config,
    attn_implementation="eager",
    dtype=torch.float32,
    **load_options,
).to(device).eval()

def encode_dna(sequence):
    sequence = sequence.strip().upper()
    if not 0 < len(sequence) <= config.max_position_embeddings:
        raise ValueError("Provide a sequence of 1 to 1,024 nucleotides.")
    if set(sequence) - set("ACGTN"):
        raise ValueError("DNA must contain only A, C, G, T or N.")
    encoded = tokenizer(sequence, return_tensors="pt", truncation=False)
    # This custom tokenizer returns 1D tensors for a single sequence.
    encoded = {
        key: value.unsqueeze(0) if value.ndim == 1 else value
        for key, value in encoded.items()
    }
    if "attention_mask" not in encoded:
        encoded["attention_mask"] = torch.ones_like(encoded["input_ids"])
    return {key: value.to(device) for key, value in encoded.items()}

sequence = "ACGTTGCATGTCGCATGATGCATGAGAGCT"
inputs = encode_dna(sequence)

with torch.inference_mode():
    outputs = model(**inputs, output_hidden_states=True, return_dict=True)
    token_embeddings = outputs.hidden_states[-1]  # [batch, length, hidden_size]

    # Optional: summarize the last-layer nucleotide embeddings by mean pooling.
    keep = inputs["attention_mask"].unsqueeze(-1).to(token_embeddings.dtype)
    sequence_embedding = (token_embeddings * keep).sum(dim=1) / keep.sum(
        dim=1
    ).clamp_min(1)

print("Last-layer token embeddings:", tuple(token_embeddings.shape))
print("Mean-pooled sequence embedding:", tuple(sequence_embedding.shape))
EOF

profile.summary: hEVO-base-o is the smaller of the two public checkpoints of hEvo, a DNA language model family from MulinLab trained on haplotype sequences from human populations. It reads a DNA sequence of up to 1,024 nucleotides and returns one 768-dimensional vector per nucleotide, plus masked-base predictions that can score a single-nucleotide variant as a log-likelihood ratio of the alternative against the reference allele. The -o checkpoints were trained on public 1000 Genomes Project and HGDP data.

sections.title: How it works
sections.body: hEVO-base-o is a bidirectional BERT-style masked language model with 12 transformer layers and hidden size 768, and one token per nucleotide with no boundary tokens. The paper describes two training stages for the family. Stage I masked 20% of valid nucleotide positions in short contiguous spans and trained the encoder and prediction head together to recover them, with cross entropy computed only at masked positions. Stage II kept the encoder fixed and updated the whole masked-language-modelling head (its dense transformation, LayerNorm and nucleotide decoder) on contexts taken from an observed alternative-allele chromosome with the focal nucleotide masked, sampled equally across five alternative-allele frequency strata. Neither stage used clinical or functional labels. For this checkpoint both stages used public 1000 Genomes and HGDP data only. To score a single-nucleotide variant, the variant site is masked once and the alternative-allele logit minus the reference-allele logit at that site gives the log-likelihood ratio. The weight file also holds tensors for an optional frequency branch, which is off by default and not built when loading.

The paper describes two training stages for the family. Stage I masked 20% of valid nucleotide positions in short contiguous spans and trained the encoder and prediction head together to recover them, with cross entropy computed only at masked positions. Stage II kept the encoder fixed and updated the whole masked-language-modelling head (its dense transformation, LayerNorm and nucleotide decoder) on contexts taken from an observed alternative-allele chromosome with the focal nucleotide masked, sampled equally across five alternative-allele frequency strata. Neither stage used clinical or functional labels. For this checkpoint both stages used public 1000 Genomes and HGDP data only. To score a single-nucleotide variant, the variant site is masked once and the alternative-allele logit minus the reference-allele logit at that site gives the log-likelihood ratio. Frequency embeddings are disabled in this checkpoint's configuration, so inference uses DNA sequence only.

steps.title: Load the model and embed a sequence
steps.shell:
python - <<'EOF'
import torch
from transformers import AutoConfig, AutoModelForMaskedLM, AutoTokenizer

REPO = "MulinLab/hEVO-large-o"
# Freeze the checkpoint and its custom code for reproducible inference.
REVISION = "09541834de8a063b09f9ddfebf06532c18bda53d"
device = torch.device("cuda" if torch.cuda.is_available() else "cpu")

load_options = dict(revision=REVISION, token=True, trust_remote_code=True)
tokenizer = AutoTokenizer.from_pretrained(REPO, **load_options)
config = AutoConfig.from_pretrained(
    REPO,
    use_frequency_embedding=False,
    use_flash_attention=False,
    **load_options,
)
assert config.use_frequency_embedding is False
model = AutoModelForMaskedLM.from_pretrained(
    REPO,
    config=config,
    attn_implementation="eager",
    dtype=torch.float32,
    **load_options,
).to(device).eval()

def encode_dna(sequence):
    sequence = sequence.strip().upper()
    if not 0 < len(sequence) <= config.max_position_embeddings:
        raise ValueError("Provide a sequence of 1 to 1,024 nucleotides.")
    if set(sequence) - set("ACGTN"):
        raise ValueError("DNA must contain only A, C, G, T or N.")
    encoded = tokenizer(sequence, return_tensors="pt", truncation=False)
    # This custom tokenizer returns 1D tensors for a single sequence.
    encoded = {
        key: value.unsqueeze(0) if value.ndim == 1 else value
        for key, value in encoded.items()
    }
    if "attention_mask" not in encoded:
        encoded["attention_mask"] = torch.ones_like(encoded["input_ids"])
    return {key: value.to(device) for key, value in encoded.items()}

sequence = "ACGTTGCATGTCGCATGATGCATGAGAGCT"
inputs = encode_dna(sequence)

with torch.inference_mode():
    outputs = model(**inputs, output_hidden_states=True, return_dict=True)
    token_embeddings = outputs.hidden_states[-1]  # [batch, length, hidden_size]

    # Optional: summarize the last-layer nucleotide embeddings by mean pooling.
    keep = inputs["attention_mask"].unsqueeze(-1).to(token_embeddings.dtype)
    sequence_embedding = (token_embeddings * keep).sum(dim=1) / keep.sum(
        dim=1
    ).clamp_min(1)

print("Last-layer token embeddings:", tuple(token_embeddings.shape))
print("Mean-pooled sequence embedding:", tuple(sequence_embedding.shape))
EOF

profile.summary: LncRFM is an RNA foundation model built for long non-coding RNAs (lncRNAs), whose function depends on both short sequence motifs and base pairing that can span thousands of nucleotides. It reads an RNA sequence and is pretrained to predict masked nucleotides, with masking guided by secondary structure; its encoder outputs can then be fine-tuned with a small task head for tasks such as lncRNA localisation, disease association or splice-site prediction. The authors also release the LncCorpus pretraining corpus and the LncBench benchmark.
profile.summary_source_locator: Europe PMC abstract; README.md: Model loading and inference, Downstream learning

sections.title: How it works
sections.body: LncRFM is a hybrid bidirectional state-space encoder: a convolutional motif stem with kernel widths 3 and 7, then 12 blocks of which ten are non-causal bidirectional selective state-space mixers and two are self-attention blocks with 12 heads, at embedding dimension 768. Pretraining is masked RNA modelling from random initialisation: 15% of non-special tokens are selected, of which 80% are replaced by [MASK], 10% by a random nucleotide and 10% left unchanged, and nucleotide reconstruction is the only objective. Predicted base pairing enters in two ways. A binary pairing indicator feeds a learnable gate that mixes the forward and reverse state-space scans. And after a warm-in phase of about 42% of the run, batches are increasingly chosen for joint masking, in which the predicted partner of a selected paired nucleotide is masked at the same time, reaching about 14.8% of batches at the end of the run and about 4% averaged over it. Downstream inference uses primary sequence alone, with the two directions simply averaged.
sections.source_locator: README.md; src/lncrfm/model/modeling_lncrfm.py; pretrain.sh; paper: Methods 4.2

sections.title: Versions and reproducibility
sections.body: One checkpoint is released: the pretrained weights at 300,000 steps in FP32, as Zenodo record 24356997, version 1.0.0, a single file LncRFM_Weights.zip (177,977,194 bytes). The archive holds a folder lncrfm_pretrained with model.safetensors, model_config.json, the tokenizer files, a README and the licence. The model settings are loaded from model_config.json, which records global step 300000 and float32 precision. A result should name the Zenodo record and version and the repository commit.

sections.title: Data and benchmark
sections.body: LncCorpus holds 24,771,981 RNA sequence and structure records in 86 Parquet files, with training and held-out partitions; the abstract says the authors contributed over 9.6 million lncRNA sequences to it. LncBench has 15 datasets and over 1,010,000 sequences across 10 tasks. The README gives one fine-tuning script per dataset, and these read the released Parquet files directly.
sections.source_locator: Zenodo 24344559 metadata; Europe PMC abstract; README.md: Downstream learning

sections.title: Training setup
sections.body: The paper reports pretraining on four data-parallel GPU processes in FP32, with a per-process microbatch of 20 and gradient accumulation of 2, so an effective batch of 160 sequences per update, over 300,000 updates. The optimiser was AdamW at a peak learning rate of 2e-4, beta1 0.9, beta2 0.999, no weight decay, 1,000 warm-up updates then linear decay, with gradients clipped at 0.5 and batches grouped by length. The GPU model and the wall-clock cost are not stated. Downstream work froze the encoder and trained only a bottleneck adapter and head, and the software stack was Python 3.9.23, PyTorch 2.3.1 and Transformers 4.44.0.
sections.source_locator: paper: Methods 4.2 Pretraining optimization; 4.3; Software and reproducibility

facts.label: Model type
facts.value: RNA foundation model for long non-coding RNAs, pretrained by masked language modelling.
facts.source_locator: Europe PMC abstract; modeling_lncrfm.py: get_lncrfm

facts.label: Architecture
facts.value: Hybrid bidirectional state-space encoder. The paper describes a multiscale convolutional motif stem with depthwise-separable branches of kernel widths 3 and 7, then 12 residual blocks: ten non-causal bidirectional selective state-space mixers (state dimension 64, local convolution width 7, expansion factor 2, head dimension 64) and two multi-head self-attention blocks with 12 heads of dimension 64. Embedding dimension 768, and no learned absolute positional embeddings. During pretraining a learnable scalar gate per block mixes the forward and reverse states according to whether a nucleotide has a predicted pairing partner; at adaptation and inference the two directions are averaged instead, from sequence alone. The paper puts the attention blocks at 6 and 12 while model_config.json lists attention layers 5 and 11, so the two sources differ.
facts.source_locator: model_config.json; src/lncrfm/model/modeling_lncrfm.py; paper: Methods 4.2

facts.label: Inputs
facts.value: An RNA sequence as nucleotide tokens, tokenised with the tokenizer shipped in the weights archive. The paper says sequences are stripped of whitespace, upper-cased and thymine is standardised to uracil, with single-nucleotide tokens plus [CLS], [SEP], [PAD], [MASK] and [UNK], a dedicated N token, and other non-canonical IUPAC symbols mapped to [UNK]. Pretraining used sequences of 200 to 2,048 nucleotides per pretrain.sh.
facts.source_locator: README.md; pretrain.sh; paper: Methods 4.1, 4.2

facts.label: Outputs
facts.value: Masked-language-model logits per token; with a task head (for example an adapter on a frozen encoder), predictions for downstream classification, regression or per-base tasks.

facts.label: Parameters
facts.value: 48.10 million in the pretrained encoder (the paper's figure, rounded to two decimals; no saved file counts the weight file), rising to 48.96 million with the downstream bottleneck adapter and binary classification head, as the paper states. In that configuration 0.825 million parameters (1.7%) are trainable, because the encoder is frozen.
facts.source_locator: paper: Methods 4.2, 4.3

facts.label: Training data
facts.value: LncCorpus: 24,771,981 RNA sequence and structure records (sequence plus pairing partners) in 86 Parquet files. The paper says it combined RNAcentral transcripts with pairing indices from the MUSES ensemble for sequences up to 512 nt and from LinearFold for longer ones, added over 9.6 million long non-coding and transcript sequences of its own to a source corpus of 31,121,367 records, and filtered that to sequences of 200 to 2,050 nt with matching sequence and pairing-vector lengths, leaving 24,648,121 pretraining sequences and 123,860 held-out validation sequences. Pretraining ran about two epochs over that corpus in 300,000 updates. CC BY 4.0 for the project's own contributions; upstream data keep their terms.

facts.value: Not reported as a date. The paper names the source databases (RNAcentral, GENCODE v47, RefSeq, LncBook 2.0, lncATLAS, POSTAR3 and others) and gives GENCODE v47 for the lncATLAS transcripts, but it does not date the RNAcentral snapshot used for pretraining.

strengths.text: Built for long transcripts: pretraining used sequences up to 2,048 nucleotides, and the masking is guided by base pairing.
Fully open: MIT code, MIT weights, and the pretraining corpus and benchmark released on Zenodo.
strengths.source_locator: LICENSE; Zenodo 24356997; README.md: Weights and data

strengths.text: Ready-made fine-tuning scripts for each LncBench dataset, plus a model test script that checks strict checkpoint loading.

The authors report the best primary-metric score on 11 of 13 adaptable LncBench datasets against seven other RNA foundation models under a frozen-encoder protocol, and that contact-prediction rankings transferred from internal human mRNAs to external human lncRNAs with a Spearman correlation of 0.90. These are the authors' claims on their own benchmark.

limitations.text: Needs an NVIDIA GPU stack for full use: the environment pins PyTorch with CUDA 11.8, the state-space kernels must be built against a matching CUDA toolkit, and the README inference example runs on CUDA.
limitations.source_locator: README.md: Installation, Model loading and inference; environment.yml

limitations.text: Very new and evaluated only by its authors: the weights were published on Zenodo on 19 November 2026 and the preprint on 22 November 2026, with a single checkpoint and no independent evaluation in the sources read. The paper also notes that its benchmark enforced a frozen-encoder protocol, so full fine-tuning was not tested, and that the base-pairing topologies in LncCorpus were computed by ensemble folding and LinearFold rather than measured.

The pretraining corpus mixes the authors' sequences with upstream data that keep their own terms, so the CC BY 4.0 licence covers only the project's own contributions. The paper lists the upstream resources separately in its data availability statement.

Human-centred and sensitive to domain shift. The paper says LncBench centres on human lncRNA assays, and that moving a human-adapted coding-potential checkpoint to the multi-kingdom RNAChallenge collection cut LncRFM's F1 from 0.929 to 0.374, with a median drop of 0.451 across the eight models tested.

steps.title: Predict a masked nucleotide
steps.shell:
python - <<'EOF'
from pathlib import Path
import json
import torch
from lncrfm import get_lncrfm, get_tokenizer

checkpoint = Path("checkpoints/lncrfm_pretrained")
options = json.loads((checkpoint / "model_config.json").read_text())["factory_kwargs"]
tokenizer = get_tokenizer(
    tokenizer_file=str(checkpoint / "tokenizer.json"),
    max_length=options["max_length"],
)
model = get_lncrfm(
    **options,
    tokenizer=tokenizer,
    from_pretrained=str(checkpoint),
    dtype=torch.float32,
    device="cuda",
).eval()

inputs = tokenizer("[CLS] A U G [MASK] C [SEP]", return_tensors="pt").to("cuda")
with torch.no_grad():

profile.summary: BulkFormer is a family of foundation models for human bulk RNA-seq. A model takes one expression profile per sample, covering about twenty thousand protein-coding genes, and returns either a single vector that represents the whole sample or a vector per gene plus recovered expression values. Those vectors are then used as frozen features for downstream prediction, for example disease classification, prognosis or drug response.
profile.summary_source_locator: README: header and Choose a model; docs/original-paper.md: Abstract; docs/architecture.md; docs/models/atlas.md

sections.title: How it works
sections.body: The three generations work differently. Atlas gives each gene a token that combines a learned identity embedding with a linear projection of log2(TPM + 1), then passes a CLS token and up to 4,096 selected gene tokens through 16 bidirectional transformer blocks of width 1,024 with 16 heads and SwiGLU feed-forward layers; the sample feature is the 1,024-dimensional CLS output taken before the projection head. Latest encodes all 19,973 gene positions at once: gene identity, a sinusoidal encoding of expression and a global expression MLP (19,973 to 2,560 to 768) are normalised separately and summed with fixed 1:1:1 coefficients, then a residual weighted graph convolution of hidden width 256 feeds a 12-layer Performer of width 768. A small network reads how much of the input is missing and applies a bounded gain and offset to the expression head. The published model of the preprint sums three embeddings per gene (an ESM2 protein embedding for identity, a rotary expression embedding of log(TPM + 1), and a sample-level MLP embedding) and passes them through three blocks of one graph convolution and four Performer layers at dimension 640. It is pretrained by masking about 15% of each sample's expression values with the placeholder -10 and minimising the mean squared error of the reconstructed values, and its gene embeddings are max-pooled to give a sample representation.
sections.source_locator: docs/architecture.md; configs; paper: Methods, BulkFormer model architecture; BulkFormer pretraining task; Downstream methods

sections.title: Versions and reproducibility
sections.body: Three generations sit in one repository. The publication family has five sizes: 37M, 50M, 93M, 127M and 147M parameters, with the authors recommending 147M where resources allow. The 2026-11-04 release added BulkFormer-Atlas (242.37M) and BulkFormer-Latest (154.55M), and on 2026-11-06 Latest moved to its final epoch-20 checkpoint. Each new model carries an immutable checkpoint ID: atlas-infonce-epoch10-update320000 and latest-20261106-epoch20-update148300. The repository is explicit that published PRIMO scores were produced by earlier checkpoints: Atlas appears as BulkFormer-variant, and the epoch-19 Latest as BulkFormer-V3Plus, whose scores do not evaluate the current download. A result should name the model, the checkpoint ID and the pooling protocol.

sections.title: Training setup of the published model
sections.body: The preprint reports pretraining on eight NVIDIA A800 GPUs for 29 epochs, about 350 GPU hours in total, with PyTorch 2.5.1, CUDA 12.4 and Python 3.12.7. The optimiser was AdamW with a maximum learning rate of 1e-4, linearly warmed up over the first 5% of steps, a per-device batch size of 4 and gradient accumulation over 128 steps. In its own comparison table the authors give an average single-GPU epoch time of about 96 hours for BulkFormer, against about 864 hours for Geneformer and about 16,128 hours for scLong. These figures describe the published model, not the later Atlas and Latest checkpoints, for which the repository gives no training cost.

facts.label: Architecture
facts.value: Atlas: 16-layer bidirectional transformer, width 1,024, 16 heads, SwiGLU, CLS readout. Latest: residual weighted GCN plus a 12-layer Performer, width 768, 12 heads, with a global expression MLP. The published model in the preprint is a third design: three stacked blocks, each one graph convolutional layer followed by four Performer layers, embedding dimension 640, eight Performer attention heads. Its gene identity embeddings come from mean-pooled ESM2 embeddings of each gene's primary protein product, its expression values are encoded by a rotary expression embedding after log(TPM + 1), and a sample context MLP embedding is added to both. The gene-gene graph is a co-expression graph keeping each gene's top 20 edges with Pearson correlation of at least 0.4.

strengths.text: It is pretrained on bulk RNA-seq rather than single-cell data. The preprint argues the modality matters, reporting that its pretraining profiles carried expression for 16,606 protein-coding genes per sample on average against 3,050 genes per cell in a single-cell dataset, and that BulkFormer outperformed the single-cell models it compared against on their downstream tasks. limitations.text: The repository says overlap between the anonymised benchmark cohorts and the pretraining data has not been fully audited, and that some downstream phenotype cohorts overlap with source collections. It also says a matched gene-level comparison between Atlas and Latest remains to be established, and that the earlier LINCS perturbation benchmark was withdrawn because the assay modality did not match bulk RNA-seq.

The authors' own limitations for the published model: it does worse than single-cell models on single-cell tasks such as cell type annotation because it was pretrained on bulk data, and it covers only protein-coding genes, with no non-coding transcripts. The preprint also reports that imputation accuracy falls as more of the input is missing, from r = 0.949 at the 15% masking rate used in pretraining to r = 0.752 at 35%, where simple statistical imputation does about as well.

profile.summary: BulkRNABert is a transformer language model for bulk RNA-seq data. It takes the expression levels of a fixed set of genes from one sample and returns embeddings of that sample. The embeddings are used to build downstream models for cancer-type classification and survival-time prediction.
profile.summary_source_locator: PMLR abstract; README.md: 1. BulkRNABert; model card: introduction

sections.title: How it works
sections.body: BulkRNABert is an encoder-only transformer. Each gene in the input is one token, and the expression value is binned on a linear scale into one of 64 bins and embedded together with a gene embedding; there is no positional encoding, because expression is permutation invariant. Pretraining follows BERT: 15% of tokens are corrupted, of which 80% become [MASK], 10% a random token and 10% are left unchanged but still counted in the loss, and the model predicts the bin of each corrupted gene. Unlike some earlier work the authors include zero expressions in the masked-language-modelling loss. The released configuration has 4 transformer layers, an embedding size of 256, 8 attention heads, 64 expression bins and 19,062 genes. For a downstream task the authors either probe the mean embedding or fine-tune with IA3, which they say adds less than 0.07% of the model's parameters.

sections.title: Versions and reproducibility
sections.body: The repository ships three pretrained checkpoints in JAX: bulk_rna_bert_tcga (pretrained on TCGA), bulk_rna_bert_gtex_encode (GTEx and ENCODE) and bulk_rna_bert_gtex_encode_tcga (a mix of all three). It also ships a classification model for five TCGA cohorts used in an example notebook. The Hugging Face repository InstaDeepAI/BulkRNABert holds a PyTorch version for the transformers library, described as pretrained on TCGA, plus the JAX parameters. A result should name the checkpoint, the framework and the commit or Hugging Face revision; this page read the repository at commit bfdc2ab8 and the Hugging Face card at revision 4ee84d56.

sections.title: Input preparation
sections.body: The model expects expression values for a fixed list of genes, given in common_gene_id.txt, in a fixed order. The repository includes a script that turns raw RNA-seq files downloaded from the GDC portal into this format, using the unstranded TPM column in its example. The Hugging Face example applies log10(1 + x) to the expression values before tokenising and checks that the number of columns equals the model's gene count.

sections.title: Training setup
sections.body: The paper reports pretraining all three models with the same hyperparameters, using AdamW with gradient accumulation to an effective batch of 3 million tokens, split across 4 TPU v4-8, for a total of 12 billion tokens. It reports reconstruction accuracies between 0.5 and 0.6 against 64 bins, and notes that accuracy was higher for the non-cancer GTEx and ENCODE data than for TCGA, which it attributes to the greater variability of expression in cancerous tissue. No training time is given.

facts.value: Transformer encoder with 4 layers, embedding size 256, 8 attention heads (key size 32) and feed-forward size 512, as the released config gives and the paper states. strengths.text: Weights for three pretraining datasets are released, so a user can compare a TCGA-only model with one trained on non-cancer tissue (GTEx and ENCODE) or a mix.
Code and weights are under Apache-2.0, and the Hugging Face weights are not gated.
The repository includes sample TCGA data, the gene list and a preprocessing script for raw GDC files, so the input format can be reproduced.

The authors report new best results on TCGA pan-cancer classification and survival analysis, and that their pan-cancer survival models keep a similar concordance index on cohorts removed from training, which they read as transfer to unseen cohorts. These are the authors' own claims. They also report that pretraining on non-cancer data alone (GTEx and ENCODE) was competitive, and that mixing non-cancer with cancer data brought no further improvement over pretraining on TCGA.

limitations.text: The input is a fixed list of genes in a fixed order, 19,062 in the released config and 19,042 in the paper. Data from another gene annotation or platform must be mapped onto this list first, and the expression values must be put on the same scale (transcripts per million, log10(1 + x), then max-normalised).
The model gives embeddings, not predictions. Classification or survival needs a downstream model; only a five-cohort classifier and a pan-cancer survival checkpoint are shipped.

limitations.text: The repository version runs in JAX with pinned versions (jax 0.4.19, dm-haiku 0.0.10). The Hugging Face version needs transformers installed from source, according to its card.

limitations.text: It was trained on bulk tissue profiles; the sources read describe no use on single-cell data. The paper's own open questions are the weaker per-cohort survival results, the lack of an interpretation method for which genes drive a prediction, and the absence of other omics sources, which earlier work found to improve both tasks.

run_guide.summary: Install the repository package at a pinned commit and compute BulkRNABert embeddings for the bundled TCGA sample with the bulk_rna_bert_tcga checkpoint.
prerequisites: Python 3.10 or later, as setup.py requires.
The package pins jax==0.4.19, jaxlib==0.4.19 and dm-haiku==0.0.10. GPU type and memory are not stated in the sources read.
Code and weights are Apache-2.0; the sample TCGA data stay under their source's terms.

steps.shell:
git clone https://github.com/instadeepai/multiomics-open-research.git
cd multiomics-open-research
git checkout --detach bfdc2ab8d7692aa6fba0f7879b4886a73ec6c700
steps.explanation: The README says to clone the repository but gives no command; the clone, cd and checkout lines are added to get the commit this page was written from. The JAX checkpoints are stored in the repository's checkpoints/ folder.

steps.shell: pip install -e .
steps.explanation: Installs the multiomics_open_research package and its pinned dependencies.

steps.title: Compute embeddings for the sample data
steps.shell:
python - <<'PY'
import haiku as hk
import jax
import jax.numpy as jnp
import pandas as pd

from multiomics_open_research.bulk_rna_bert.pretrained import get_bulkrnabert_pretrained_model
from multiomics_open_research.common.preprocess import preprocess_omic

# Get pretrained model
parameters, forward_fn, tokenizer, config = get_bulkrnabert_pretrained_model(
    model_name="bulk_rna_bert_tcga",
    embeddings_layers_to_save=(4,),
    checkpoint_directory="checkpoints/",
)
forward_fn = hk.transform(forward_fn)

# Get bulk RNASeq data and tokenize it
gene_expression_df = pd.read_csv("data/bulkrnabert/tcga_sample.csv")
gene_expression_array = preprocess_omic(gene_expression_df, config)
gene_expression_ids = tokenizer.batch_tokenize(gene_expression_array)
gene_expression_ids = jnp.asarray(gene_expression_ids, dtype=jnp.int32)

# Inference
random_key = jax.random.PRNGKey(0)
outs = forward_fn.apply(parameters, random_key, gene_expression_ids)

# Get mean embeddings from layer 4
gene_expression_mean_embeddings = outs["embeddings_4"].mean(axis=1)
PY
steps.explanation: The README inference snippet, wrapped in a shell heredoc and run from the repository root. Replace bulk_rna_bert_tcga with bulk_rna_bert_gtex_encode or bulk_rna_bert_gtex_encode_tcga to use the other checkpoints.

outputs: An array of mean layer-4 embeddings, one row per sample in tcga_sample.csv, held in memory. The snippet prints nothing and writes no file.
limitations: These commands were read from the repository and have not been executed by Rewire.
The guide stops at embeddings. Classification or survival prediction needs a downstream model, as in the repository's example notebook.
Own data must first be converted to the model's gene list, for example with scripts/preprocess_tcga_rna_seq.py for GDC files.

profile.summary: Ladon is a foundation model for bulk RNA sequencing of tumours, built by the company Blank Bio. It learns from millions of RNA-seq profiles by reconstructing masked parts of isoform-level expression, and its embeddings are then used to predict patient survival, recurrence and response to treatment. The developers present it as a way to make RNA-based predictions that still hold in clinical trials and cohorts the model was not fitted on.
profile.summary_source_locator: Report page 1 (abstract); page 2, Introducing Ladon

sections.title: How it works
sections.body: Ladon is a transformer encoder-decoder of 3 billion parameters. It is pretrained self-supervised, by masked token reconstruction on isoform-level expression profiles, so it can learn from samples without outcome labels. For clinical use the developers then mid-train it with supervision to predict patient and tumour characteristics such as disease stage, age, tumour grade and genomic alterations, together with clinical outcomes. They then discard the prediction heads, freeze the encoder and fit simple outcome models, such as linear Cox survival models, on its embeddings. The report does not describe the layers, tokenisation or training corpus in more detail.
sections.source_locator: Report page 2, Introducing Ladon; page 11, Methods: Ladon representations; page 6; page 28, Methods

sections.title: Versions and reproducibility
sections.body: The report describes one model family and several adaptations of it (pretrained encoder, supervised mid-training with survival or response labels), and shows models of several sizes and training steps in its scaling figures, but names no released checkpoint. No weights, code or data release is listed with the report. On 2026-11-26 the GitHub organisation blankbio had 0 public repositories and the Hugging Face organisation BlankBio had 0 models and 0 datasets. Results from Ladon cannot be reproduced independently from public material.
sections.source_locator: Report pages 11, 41 to 42 (Figures 20 and 21, Methods: Reconstruction loss); GitHub org API; Hugging Face org overview

sections.title: Evaluation in the report
sections.body: Every result is reported on a setting not used for fitting: a held-out trial, another cohort or another platform. Survival models fitted on TCGA were applied unchanged to CPTAC and the reverse; the developers report Ladon ahead of differential gene expression signatures, BulkRNABERT and BulkFormer, and that adding Ladon to clinical covariates improved survival prediction in all 12 target cohorts. They also report better response prediction for immunotherapy than PD-L1 expression, recovery of isoform usage from gene-level counts (median Pearson r of 0.81 across 3,000 genes in held-out tumours), and cell-composition inference from single-cell references. For the scaling claim they assembled their own patient-level benchmark, ClinBench, aggregating 142 tasks across survival, treatment response and patient and tumour characteristics, and report that lower pretraining reconstruction loss went with better average performance on it, with reconstruction loss still falling at the largest size tested. All of these are the developers' own results in an unreviewed report.

profile.summary: Akita predicts how a stretch of DNA folds in three dimensions. It takes just over one megabase of sequence, one-hot encoded, and returns a predicted contact map for that window, as log observed over expected values, for each of five cell types it was trained on. It is used for in silico work: saturation mutagenesis, interpreting eQTLs, predicting the effect of structural variants and comparing species.
profile.summary_source_locator: Paper abstract (Europe PMC record); params.json: model; targets.txt; explore_model.ipynb

sections.title: How it works
sections.body: Akita is a convolutional network in two halves. A 1D trunk reads the one-hot sequence: a convolution block with 96 filters of size 11 by 4, then a tower of ten convolution and pooling blocks with 96 filters of width 5, then eight dilated residual blocks and a width-1 bottleneck convolution with 64 filters, which brings 1,048,576 bases down to 512 representations of 2,048 bp bins. A 2D head averages the representations of each pair of bins, concatenates an encoding of the distance between them, symmetrises, applies six dilated 2D residual blocks, crops the edges and reads off the upper triangle with a diagonal offset of 2. The final layer has five linear units, one per training dataset. Training minimised mean squared error on the upper triangle with stochastic gradient descent with momentum, batches of 2 sequences, for about 60 epochs, stopping when validation loss had not improved for 12 epochs. Each sequence was stochastically shifted by up to 11 bp and reverse complemented with its map flipped. A Bayesian search with Dragonfly chose a learning rate of 0.0065, momentum 0.99575 and gradient clipping 10.7. The published model has 751,653 parameters, of which 746,149 are trainable.
sections.source_locator: params.json; keras_print.txt; paper: Online Methods, Model architecture and Training Approach

sections.title: Versions and reproducibility
sections.body: There are two generations. The published model is a single TensorFlow checkpoint, model_best.h5, trained on human Hi-C and micro-C mapped to hg38 at 2048 bp resolution, with params.json as its configuration. In 2021 the authors retrained Akita on human and mouse data together after a further hyperparameter search, splitting the genome into eight folds and training one model per held-out fold; those data and models sit in Google Cloud Storage under gs://basenji_hic/3-2021, with model file suffix 0 for human and 1 for mouse. A result should say which generation and, for the 2021 set, which fold and species. This page read the repository at commit 06ce5d38.
sections.source_locator: manuscripts/akita/README.md: Manuscript model and data; v2/README.md; get_model.sh

sections.title: Reported accuracy
sections.body: The authors report, on their held-out test set, a mean squared error of 0.14, a Pearson correlation of 0.61 and a Spearman correlation of 0.56 genome-wide, and say this approaches the limit set by noise between experimental replicates. They also report that training on all five datasets together was more accurate than training on single datasets, but that the model predicted limited cell-type-specific differences, which they attribute to how few loci show strong cell-type differences in current experiments. For mouse sequence, the human-trained model reached a median Spearman correlation of 0.50 against mouse ESC Hi-C, and a model trained on mouse data reached 0.63. These are the authors' own figures.
sections.source_locator: paper: Results

facts.label: Model type
facts.value: Supervised convolutional neural network predicting contact maps from DNA sequence.
facts.source_locator: Paper abstract; basenji README: Akita

facts.label: Architecture
facts.value: 1D trunk feeding a 2D head, with 5 linear output units. The paper gives the layers: a convolution with 96 filters of size 11 by 4 on the one-hot sequence with batch normalisation, ReLU and width-2 max pooling; a convolution tower repeating 96 filters of width 5 with the same pooling until the sequence is 512 representations of 2048 bp windows; a dilated residual convolution tower with geometrically increasing dilation and dropout; and a width-1 bottleneck convolution with 64 filters. The head averages the representations of every pair of bins i and j, concatenates a positional encoding of the distance between them, applies a 2D dilated residual tower that re-symmetrises at each iteration with a Symmetrize2D layer, and ends in a linear transformation that predicts all five datasets at once.
facts.source_locator: params.json; paper: Online Methods, Model architecture

facts.value: One-hot encoded DNA of length 1,048,576 bases (2^20), shaped [regions, 1048576, 4].

facts.value: 751,653 total, 746,149 trainable and 5,504 non-trainable, in the published model as printed by Keras. The paper states the same 746,149 trainable parameters.

facts.label: Training data
facts.value: Five human contact maps at 2048 bp resolution on hg38: HFF and H1hESC micro-C from Krietenstein 2019, GM12878 and IMR90 in situ Hi-C from Rao 2014, and HCT116 from Rao 2017. The paper says these were reprocessed with distiller to map to hg38 and cooler for genome-wide iterative correction, then adaptively coarse-grained, normalised for distance, log-transformed, clipped to (-2, 2), interpolated over missing bins and smoothed with a small 2D Gaussian filter. The genome was cut at assembly gaps and unmappable regions into 10 Mb virtual contigs, assigned 80/10/10 to training, validation and test, giving 7,008 training, 419 validation and 413 test sequences. The paper also trained a separate mouse (mm10) model on Hi-C from Bonev 2017 and micro-C from Hsieh, and the 2021 models train human and mouse together.

strengths.text: Small model, about 750 thousand parameters, and the authors say that while training was computationally intensive, the effects of sequence changes could be predicted in seconds, which is what makes in silico saturation mutagenesis and variant scoring practical.
One forward pass gives maps for five cell types at once, so cell-type differences can be read from the same prediction.

Code, model configuration and a notebook that predicts from an arbitrary sequence are published in the Apache-2.0 Basenji repository, with scripts that download the weights and training data (no licence is stated for those files), and the repository also holds the training scripts.
strengths.source_locator: LICENSE; manuscripts/akita/README.md: get_model.sh, get_data.sh, Train new models; get_model.sh; explore_model.ipynb

limitations.text: The window is fixed at 2^20 bases and the output is binned to 2048 bp, so interactions beyond about one megabase are out of reach and the notebook refuses sequences of any other length. The authors state that the model is not influenced by information beyond the window, and that features visible between chromosomes, such as A/B compartmentalisation, are left to future work.

The published checkpoint covers five human cell types only, all on hg38. For mouse the paper trained a separate mm10 model, and the 2021 release has one model per fold for human and for mouse. The authors also note that the model must be trained on Hi-C or micro-C data for any cell type where sequence perturbation predictions are wanted, and that cell-type specificity of its predictions needs further work.
limitations.source_locator: data/targets.txt; v2 README; paper: Results; Discussion; Online Methods, Mouse model training

limitations.text: It runs inside the Basenji codebase and is installed from requirements.txt or a conda environment, with TensorFlow installed separately, plus cooltools for the notebook. There is no pip package for Akita itself.

run_guide.summary: Install Basenji, download the trained Akita model, and predict a contact map for one megabase of hg38 sequence.
prerequisites: Python 3 with the Basenji dependencies from environment.yml or requirements.txt, and TensorFlow installed separately (the README says the codebase works with the latest TensorFlow 2 and should also work with 1.15).
cooltools for the exploration notebook, installed with pip.
pysam and a copy of hg38 (the notebook downloads hg38.ml.fa.gz from basenji_barnyard2 if it is missing).
The notebook sets CUDA_VISIBLE_DEVICES to -1, so it runs on CPU. GPU memory needs are not stated in the sources read.
Code is Apache-2.0.

steps.title: Load the model and predict from a sequence
steps.shell:
python - <<'PY'
import json, os, subprocess
os.environ["CUDA_VISIBLE_DEVICES"] = '-1' ### run on CPU
import numpy as np
import pysam
from basenji import dna_io, seqnn

with open('params.json') as params_open:
    params = json.load(params_open)
    params_model = params['model']

seqnn_model = seqnn.SeqNN(params_model)
seqnn_model.restore('model_best.h5')
print('successfully loaded')

os.makedirs('./data', exist_ok=True)
if not os.path.isfile('./data/hg38.ml.fa'):
    print('downloading hg38.ml.fa')
    subprocess.call('curl -o ./data/hg38.ml.fa.gz https://storage.googleapis.com/basenji_barnyard2/hg38.ml.fa.gz', shell=True)
    subprocess.call('gunzip ./data/hg38.ml.fa.gz', shell=True)

fasta_open = pysam.Fastafile('./data/hg38.ml.fa')
seq = fasta_open.fetch('chr12', 115163136, 116211712).upper()
seq_1hot = dna_io.dna_1hot(seq)
test_pred_from_seq = seqnn_model.model.predict(np.expand_dims(seq_1hot,0))
print(test_pred_from_seq.shape)
PY

The region chr12:115163136-116211712 is one of the notebook's own example test regions, which is 2^20 bases long. The makedirs line and the final print of the output shape are additions.

profile.summary: Puffin-D is a deep learning model that predicts transcription initiation signals from DNA sequence. It takes 100 kbp of genome sequence and returns base-level predictions for ten tracks: five assays that map transcription start sites (FANTOM CAGE, ENCODE CAGE, ENCODE RAMPAGE, GRO-cap and PRO-cap) on each strand. It is the prediction-focused companion of Puffin, an interpretable model from the same authors.
profile.summary_source_locator: README.md: introduction; Puffin-D

sections.title: How it works
sections.body: Puffin-D is a fully convolutional network. One-hot DNA passes through a stack of strided 1D convolutions that downsample the sequence by factors of 4, 4, 5, 5, 5 and 2, each followed by residual convolution blocks. Upsampling layers with skip connections then restore base resolution. This down-and-up pass is repeated a second time; the paper says the two passes allow better mixing of global and local information. A final 1x1 convolution with a softplus gives 10 non-negative output tracks at each position. Puffin-D is trained on 100 kb intervals sampled at random from the training chromosomes, with a pseudo-Poisson loss, to predict the exact level of the signal rather than only its shape.
sections.source_locator: puffin_D.py: model class; paper Materials and Methods: Prediction-focused Puffin-D model for transcription initiation

sections.title: Puffin and Puffin-D
sections.body: The repository holds two models. Puffin is an interpretation-focused model that explains each transcription start site in terms of motifs and single bases, and works on short sequences with 325 bp padding on each side. Puffin-D is the deep learning model for prediction over 100 kbp. The README says Puffin-D gives better predictions when prediction is the main need.

profile.summary: DeepSTARR predicts how strongly a 249 base pair piece of DNA acts as an enhancer in Drosophila melanogaster S2 cells. It is a convolutional neural network with two outputs, one for developmental and one for housekeeping enhancer activity, trained on genome-wide UMI-STARR-seq measurements. Besides prediction, it is used to read out which nucleotides drive the predicted activity and so to study transcription factor motifs and their syntax.
profile.summary_source_locator: README: DeepSTARR, DeepSTARR model; preprint abstract; DeepSTARR.model.json: input layer and output layers

sections.title: How it works
sections.body: The architecture is adapted from Basset: four convolutional layers, each followed by batch normalisation, a ReLU activation and max pooling, then two fully connected layers of 256 units and two single-unit output layers, Dense_Dev and Dense_Hk. The released model file gives 256 filters of width 7 in the first convolutional layer, then 60 of width 3, 60 of width 5 and 120 of width 3, with pooling size 2 throughout; the paper's methods give 246 filters for the first layer, so the two sources differ on that one number. The convolutional layers pick up local motifs and motif syntax; the fully connected layers combine them into one activity value per enhancer type. The model is a regression on measured UMI-STARR-seq activity, not a classifier. The paper trained it in Keras 2.2.4 with TensorFlow 1.14.0, the Adam optimiser at learning rate 0.002, mean squared error loss, batch size 128 and early stopping with a patience of ten epochs.
sections.source_locator: DeepSTARR.model.json; paper Methods: DeepSTARR model architecture and training

sections.title: Interpreting the model
sections.body: The repository ships a second script that computes nucleotide contribution scores for a given sequence, separately for developmental or housekeeping activity, using DeepLIFT and SHAP. A Colab notebook runs the whole path end to end: training, contribution scores and TF-MoDISco motifs. The preprint states that the model learned TF motifs and higher-order syntax rules, including the effect of motif-flanking sequence and inter-motif distances, and that these rules were validated experimentally.

profile.summary: BioFM is a genomic foundation model from M42 Health that reads DNA together with biological context. Its BioToken tokeniser encodes genetic variants and annotated regions (such as genes and regulatory elements) directly in the input, instead of treating DNA as bases only. The model produces embeddings for variants or sequences, which are used with simple classifiers to predict effects on expression, splicing and pathogenicity; it can also generate DNA sequence.
profile.summary_source_locator: Europe PMC abstract; model card: Model Details; README: Quick Start

sections.title: How it works
sections.body: BioFM is a decoder-only (causal) transformer on the Mistral architecture, with 23 layers and hidden size 640. The paper says the authors kept Mistral's grouped-query attention, disabled its sliding-window attention so the model sees the whole input, and raised the RoPE frequency parameter to handle longer DNA. Its input is DNA annotated with BioTokens: special variant tokens replace the standard bases at single nucleotide variants and insertions, and further tokens mark transcript boundaries, exons and coding sequences. During pretraining, half of the inputs were reverse complemented. For a variant, the package builds an upstream and a downstream sequence, each ending at the variant and half the evaluation context long; the downstream one is reverse complemented. Reference and mutated embeddings are each averaged over the two directions and then concatenated, giving a vector twice the embedding size. For plain sequences the embedding is taken from the last token. Downstream predictions use linear probing on these embeddings.
sections.source_locator: config.json; README: Usage; paper Results (BioToken, BioFM) and Appendix A.2

sections.body: One checkpoint is released: m42-health/BioFM-265M. A result should name it and its Hugging Face revision; this page read revision 52218bbd. The biofm-eval package is version 0.1.0. The README includes a script to reproduce the paper's variant benchmark by linear probing on the m42-health/variant-benchmark dataset with chromosome-based folds. Training ran on an NVIDIA DGX cluster with H100 GPUs using PyTorch FSDP. The paper's ablations used a smaller 67M-parameter model, which is not among the released checkpoints in the saved files; the paper says the training code is adapted from Meta's llama-cookbook.

profile.summary: Genomics-FM is a DNA foundation model meant to cut the amount of labelled data that genomic prediction tasks need. It is a BERT-style encoder pretrained on large amounts of unlabelled DNA with an ensemble of tokenisation vocabularies (BPE and 6-mer), then fine-tuned with one task-specific vocabulary on a small labelled set. The authors apply it to genome annotation, epigenomic and expression profile prediction, and variant effect assessment.
profile.summary_source_locator: Europe PMC abstract; srun_pretrain.py; srun_pretrain.sh

sections.title: How it works
sections.body: The model is a BERT masked language model built on the MosaicML BERT code, which uses ALiBi position biases and FlashAttention. During pretraining each sequence is tokenised either with a BPE vocabulary or as overlapping 6-mers, and a prompt token marking the vocabulary ([BPE] or [KMER]) and the position scheme ([ALIBI] or [APE]) is put in front of it. Sequences are randomly replaced by their reverse complement half the time. Training masks tokens with a probability of 0.15 for BPE input and 0.15 divided by 6 for 6-mer input, over blocks of 512 tokens, for up to 1,000,000 steps in fp16; the paper adds that 6-mer masking covers at least six consecutive tokens to prevent information leakage. The paper says ALiBi lets the model take downstream inputs longer than the pretraining inputs. For a downstream task the model is fine-tuned with one chosen vocabulary.
sections.source_locator: configuration_bert.py; srun_pretrain.py (CSVIterableDataset, arguments); srun_pretrain.sh; Europe PMC abstract

profile.summary: GROVER is a DNA language model pretrained on the human genome. It splits DNA into variable-length tokens learned by byte-pair encoding, and turns a DNA sequence into contextual embeddings. Its authors intend it as a foundation model that is fine-tuned for a specific task, such as promoter identity or protein-DNA binding.
profile.summary_source_locator: bioRxiv abstract; tutorial notebook, Overview

sections.title: How it works
sections.body: GROVER is a BERT model for masked language modelling: 12 layers, hidden size 768, 12 attention heads and a vocabulary of 609 tokens. The vocabulary comes from byte-pair encoding of the human genome: the authors trained models on vocabularies from 100 to 5,000 BPE cycles and picked cycle 600 with a next-k-mer prediction task. In pretraining, 2.2% of the tokens in each input are selected for prediction, most of them replaced by a mask token. The paper says pretraining used more than 5 million samples from the genome, on A100 GPUs, with the Adam optimiser and batches of 64. Because byte-pair tokens depend on the surrounding sequence, a short sequence can be tokenised differently from the same stretch in the whole genome; the card advises adding 100 nucleotides at each end. For a task, the pretrained model is loaded with a classification head and fine-tuned on labelled sequences.
sections.source_locator: config.json; model card; paper Results and Methods: The DLM GROVER

sections.title: Versions and reproducibility
sections.body: One pretrained checkpoint is published, on Hugging Face as PoetschLab/GROVER and on Zenodo (record 8373117, which also holds the optimizer and scheduler state). The tokenised genome, hg19, which some fine-tuning tasks need, is a separate Zenodo deposit. The code used in the paper is deposited on Zenodo rather than in a code repository. A result should name the checkpoint revision and the tokenisation used for the input sequences.
