steps.title: Fine-tune on the CTCF example and evaluate
steps.shell:
python - <<'PY'
import pandas as pd
import wget
import os
import numpy as np

from sklearn.metrics import matthews_corrcoef, accuracy_score, precision_score, recall_score, f1_score

import transformers
from transformers import AutoTokenizer, Trainer, AutoModelForSequenceClassification, TrainingArguments
from torch.utils.data import Dataset

CTCF_dataset_url = "https://datashare.tu-dresden.de/s/pjb5gcWGGrbcARN/download/CTCF_dataset.tsv"
file_name = "CTCF_dataset.tsv"
if os.path.exists(file_name):
  os.remove(file_name) # if exists, remove it directly
file_name = wget.download(CTCF_dataset_url, out=file_name)

CTCF_dataset = pd.read_csv('CTCF_dataset.tsv', sep='\t')
train = CTCF_dataset.sample(frac=0.8, random_state=0)
validation = CTCF_dataset.drop(train.index)
test = validation.sample(frac=0.5, random_state=0)
validation = validation.drop(test.index)
train = train.reset_index(drop=True)
validation = validation.reset_index(drop=True)
test = test.reset_index(drop=True)

tokenizer = AutoTokenizer.from_pretrained("PoetschLab/GROVER")
model = AutoModelForSequenceClassification.from_pretrained("PoetschLab/GROVER")

class SupervisedDataset(Dataset):
    """Dataset for supervised fine-tuning."""
    def __init__(self, texts, labels, tokenizer):
        super(SupervisedDataset, self).__init__()
        sequences = [text for text in texts]
        output = tokenizer(
            sequences,
            add_special_tokens=True,
            max_length=310,
            padding="longest",
            return_tensors="pt",
            truncation=True
        )
        self.input_ids = output["input_ids"]
        self.attention_mask = output["attention_mask"]
        self.labels = labels
    def __len__(self):
        return len(self.input_ids)
    def __getitem__(self, i):
        return dict(
            input_ids=self.input_ids[i],
            labels=self.labels[i],
            attention_mask=self.attention_mask[i]
        )

train_dataset = SupervisedDataset(train.sequence, train.label, tokenizer)
test_dataset = SupervisedDataset(test.sequence, test.label, tokenizer)
val_dataset = SupervisedDataset(validation.sequence, validation.label, tokenizer)

def calculate_metric_with_sklearn(logits: np.ndarray, labels: np.ndarray):
    predictions = np.argmax(logits, axis=-1)
    return {
        "accuracy": accuracy_score(labels, predictions),
        "f1": f1_score(labels, predictions, average="macro", zero_division=0),
        "matthews_correlation": matthews_corrcoef(labels, predictions),
        "precision": precision_score(labels, predictions, average="macro", zero_division=0),
        "recall": recall_score(labels, predictions, average="macro", zero_division=0),
    }

def compute_metrics(eval_pred):
    logits, labels = eval_pred
    if isinstance(logits, tuple):  # Unpack logits if it's a tuple
        logits = logits[0]
    return calculate_metric_with_sklearn(logits, labels)

train_args = TrainingArguments(seed = 42,
                               output_dir=".",
                               per_device_train_batch_size=16,
                               eval_strategy="epoch",
                               learning_rate=0.000001,
                               num_train_epochs=4
                               )
trainer = transformers.Trainer(
                                model=model,
                                tokenizer=tokenizer,
                                compute_metrics=compute_metrics,
                                train_dataset=train_dataset,
                                eval_dataset=val_dataset,
                                args = train_args
                                )
trainer.train()
results = trainer.evaluate(eval_dataset=test_dataset)
print(results)
PY

profile.summary: LucaOne is a biological foundation model that reads nucleic acid (DNA or RNA) and protein sequences with one shared model. Given a sequence and its type, it returns an embedding: a matrix with one vector per residue or a single vector for the whole sequence. These embeddings are used as inputs to downstream models for sequence-level or residue-level classification and regression.
profile.summary_source_locator: README.md: title, TimeLine 2025/12/31; LucaOneApp README: embedding methods and parameters

sections.title: How it works
sections.body: LucaOne (also called LucaGPLM) is a transformer encoder over a joint vocabulary of nucleotides and amino acids. The paper says it uses pre-layer normalisation, rotary position embeddings in place of absolute positions so that longer sequences can be inferred, and a token-type code that marks nucleotides as 0 and amino acids as 1. Pretraining is semi-supervised: two masked-token tasks (Gene-Mask and Prot-Mask) plus eight tasks that predict annotations, such as genome region type, order-level taxonomy, protein keywords and C-alpha structure coordinates. The published default checkpoint has 20 layers, hidden size 2560, 40 attention heads and a 39-token vocabulary. Each input is marked as gene (DNA or RNA) or prot. The output is the last hidden layer: per-token vectors including [CLS] and [SEP], which can be pooled to one vector by mean, [CLS] or trainable attention pooling. Long sequences are split into overlapping fragments and the embeddings merged.
sections.source_locator: config.json; README; paper Results and Methods: Model architecture, Pre-training tasks details

sections.title: Versions and reproducibility
sections.body: Checkpoints are named by training step. The README recommends lucaone at step 36000000, 17600000 or 5600000 for both nucleic acid and protein, lucaone-gene at step 36800000 for DNA and RNA only, and lucaone-prot at step 30000000 for protein only. The paper's evaluations use the 5.6 million step checkpoint (trained on 36.95 billion tokens), and the paper also describes releasing the 17.6 million step checkpoint; it trained LucaOne-Gene and LucaOne-Prot as comparison models. The original code downloads checkpoints from the developers' FTP server by --llm_type, --llm_version and --llm_step, and the paper deposits checkpoints and an archived copy of the code on Zenodo (10.5281/zenodo.15171943). Since 2025 they are also on Hugging Face under LucaGroup, loaded with the lucaone package (version 1.1.1 for the card read). A result should name the checkpoint and step, the route (FTP, Zenodo or Hugging Face) and the Hugging Face revision; this page read LucaOne-default-step36M at revision f0d2807e.

strengths.text: Long sequences are handled by overlapping fragments, and the code falls back to CPU when GPU memory runs out.

Weights are MIT licensed on the model card; code is Apache-2.0. The weights are not gated.

steps.title: Embed a nucleotide sequence
steps.shell:
python - <<'PY'
import torch
import lucaone
from transformers import AutoTokenizer, AutoModel, TrainingArguments, Trainer

# model_id
model_id = "LucaGroup/LucaOne-default-step36M"

tokenizer = AutoTokenizer.from_pretrained(
    model_id,
    trust_remote_code=True,
    force_download=True
)

model = AutoModel.from_pretrained(
    model_id,
    task_level="token_level",
    task_type="embedding",
    trust_remote_code=True,
    force_download=True
)

# device
device = torch.device("cuda" if torch.cuda.is_available() else "cpu")
model.to(device)
model.eval()

# nucleotide sequence
nucleotide_sequence = "ATGCGTACGTTAGC"
nucleotide_inputs = tokenizer(
    nucleotide_sequence,
    # note: gene sequence(for DNA or RNA), seq_type must be 'gene'
    seq_type="gene",
    return_tensors="pt",
    add_special_tokens=True
)
new_nucleotide_inputs = {}
for item in nucleotide_inputs.items():
    new_nucleotide_inputs[item[0]] = item[1].to(device)
nucleotide_inputs = new_nucleotide_inputs

with torch.no_grad():
    nucleotide_outputs = model(**nucleotide_inputs)
    # last hidden matrix as embedding matrix: [batch_size, seq_len + 2, hidden_size]
    nucleotide_last_hidden = nucleotide_outputs.last_hidden_state
    # mean pooling
    mean_nucleotide_embedding = nucleotide_last_hidden[:, 1:-1, :].mean(dim=1)
print(f"Nucleotide Embedding Shape: {nucleotide_last_hidden.shape}")
print(mean_nucleotide_embedding)
PY
steps.explanation: The model card's feature-extraction example, wrapped in a shell heredoc and shortened: the protein half and some intermediate print lines are left out. Use seq_type="prot" for a protein sequence, as the card shows.

outputs: The shape of the embedding matrix, [batch_size, seq_len + 2, hidden_size], and the mean-pooled embedding vector.

profile.summary: AIDO.DNA, now renamed GB.DNA by its developer GenBio AI, is a large DNA language model meant as a general-purpose encoder of DNA sequence. It reads up to 4,000 nucleotides one base at a time and was pretrained on 10.6 billion nucleotides from 796 species. Its embeddings are fine-tuned or probed for tasks such as gene expression prediction, genome mining, in silico mutagenesis and sequence generation.
profile.summary_source_locator: bioRxiv abstract; model card: introduction, Tokenization; ModelGenerator backbones: deprecated aliases

sections.title: How it works
sections.body: AIDO.DNA is a BERT-style, encoder-only dense transformer trained with masked language modelling: 15% of tokens in each sequence are chosen, of which 80% are masked. It uses single-nucleotide tokens from a 5-letter vocabulary (A, T, C, G, N), with a [CLS] token at the start and an [EOS] token at the end of each sequence. The authors updated the BERT design with SwiGLU, LayerNorms and rotary positional embeddings (RoPE). The 7B model has 32 layers, 32 attention heads and hidden size 4352; the paper gives the 300M model 24 layers, 16 heads, embedding size 1,024 and feed-forward size 2,688. Its design bet, in the authors' words, is to scale model size while keeping a short 4k context. The 7B model was trained for 100000 iterations at global batch size 1024 on 256 H100 GPUs with Megatron-LM, which took 8 days; the paper says the 300M model trained for 4 days on 32 A100 GPUs.
sections.source_locator: GB.DNA-7B model card; paper section 2 (Architecture, Training, Optimization)

sections.title: Versions and reproducibility
sections.body: Two pretrained checkpoints are released: a 7B model and a 300M model. Both were first published as AIDO.DNA-7B and AIDO.DNA-300M and are now named GB.DNA-7B and GB.DNA-300M on Hugging Face. The API responses saved here were requested under the old names and came back with the new repository ids. In ModelGenerator the backbones are gb_dna_7b and gb_dna_300m, and the old names aido_dna_7b and aido_dna_300m remain as deprecated aliases. The 300M card gives no training details of its own and refers to the 7B card. A result should name the checkpoint and its revision; this page read GB.DNA-7B at 5dd948f7 and GB.DNA-300M at a833c560.
sections.source_locator: Hugging Face API responses (requested by old name); ModelGenerator backbones; 300M model card

sections.title: Evaluation in the paper
sections.body: The authors evaluated the 7B model on supervised, generative and zero-shot tasks in functional genomics, synthetic biology and drug development, choosing hyperparameters on a 10% validation split. They report that it outperforms earlier encoder-only DNA models without using new data, and argue that new scaling laws are needed for compute-optimal DNA language models. On one task they report the 300M model doing best, which they attribute to its smaller embedding size. These are the authors' claims.

profile.summary: PhyloGPN is a convolutional network that reads DNA sequence alone and outputs, for every position, the parameters of a nucleotide substitution model (Felsenstein's F81). It was trained to fit those parameters to columns of the Zoonomia multispecies whole-genome alignment given a phylogenetic tree, which makes the output a statement about how constrained each site is. It needs no alignment at prediction time, so it can score variants and supply embeddings from a single sequence.
profile.summary_source_locator: docs/models/phylogpn.md opening paragraph; model card first paragraph; arXiv abstract

sections.title: How it works
sections.body: The network is convolutional, adapted from the CARP protein model: 20 stacks of 2 layers (the paper counts 40 residual blocks) with kernel size 5, inner dimension 480 and outer dimension 960, dilated to a receptive field of 481 positions. Its weights are constrained so that predictions are reverse-complement equivariant. It is trained to maximise the likelihood of each alignment column under a phylogenetic tree: the output at a position gives the F81 rate parameters for that site, and the stationary distribution of that substitution process says how viable each allele is there. Because the tree and alignment enter only through the loss, prediction takes plain sequence. The model works as a sliding window: an input of length l yields outputs for the l minus 480 central positions, so sequences are padded before scoring. The paper also describes PhyloGPN-X, which pools embeddings of neighbouring positions to give an effective receptive field of 6,001 bp.
sections.source_locator: config.json; model card; paper sections 3.3 and 3.4

sections.title: Versions and reproducibility
sections.body: One checkpoint is published, songlab/PhyloGPN, read here at revision a763739c. It is one of four model families in the songlab-cal/gpn package, which supports PhyloGPN for inference only, not training or fine-tuning, and reaches it through AutoClass APIs rather than the gpn command line. The checkpoint ships its own modelling code, so loading needs trust_remote_code. A result should name the checkpoint revision, the padding used and the window conventions.

python - <<'PY'
from gpn import register_auto_classes
from transformers import AutoModel

register_auto_classes("phylo")

model = AutoModel.from_pretrained("songlab/PhyloGPN")
print(model.config)
PY
steps.explanation: The documentation's quick start, wrapped in a heredoc, with a print of the configuration added to confirm the load. This is one of two loading routes: the package registers the AutoClasses for you. Note that pip install gpn is not pinned to the commit read for this page.

steps.title: Score a batch of sequences
steps.shell:
python - <<'PY'
import torch
from transformers import AutoModel, AutoTokenizer

checkpoint = "songlab/PhyloGPN"
tokenizer = AutoTokenizer.from_pretrained(checkpoint, trust_remote_code=True)
model = AutoModel.from_pretrained(checkpoint, trust_remote_code=True)

# Example data
seqs = [
    "TATAAA",
    "GGCCAATCT",
    "CACGTG",
    "AGGTCACGT",
    "GCCAGCC",
    "GGGGATTTCC"
]

# Output length is input length minus 480 (the receptive field size minus 1)
pad_token = tokenizer.pad_token
pad_size = 481 // 2
pad_sequence = lambda seq: pad_token * pad_size + seq + pad_token * pad_size
padded_seqs = [pad_sequence(seq) for seq in seqs]
input_tensor = tokenizer(padded_seqs, return_tensors="pt", padding=True)["input_ids"]

with torch.no_grad():
    padded_embeddings = model.get_embeddings(input_tensor)
    padded_logits = model(input_tensor) # These are log rate parameters for the F81 model

embeddings = []
logits = []

for i in range(len(seqs)):
    length = len(seqs[i])
    embeddings.append(padded_embeddings[i, :length])
    logits.append({})

    for k in "ACGT":
        logits[-1][k] = padded_logits[k][i, :length]

print(embeddings[0].shape, {k: v.shape for k, v in logits[0].items()})
PY
steps.explanation: The model card's example, wrapped in a heredoc, with a print of the first sequence's embedding and logit shapes added. It pads each sequence so that outputs cover every input position. This is the second loading route: it skips the gpn package and loads the checkpoint's own code with trust_remote_code, so it can be run instead of the previous step.

outputs: For each input sequence: a per-position embedding tensor, and a log rate parameter per position for each of A, C, G and T.

profile.summary: ProtBert is a protein language model with the BERT architecture, trained only on protein sequences with a masked language modelling objective: 15 per cent of the amino acids in a sequence are hidden and the model learns to put them back. It takes an uppercase amino-acid sequence, written with a space between residues, and returns either predictions for the masked positions or a vector per residue, 1024 numbers wide, that can be used as a feature for another model. The developers say it can be used for feature extraction or fine-tuned on a downstream task, and that fine-tuning was more accurate on some tasks.
profile.summary_source_locator: Model card: ProtBert model, Model description, Intended uses & limitations, How to use; config.json

sections.title: How it works
sections.body: The architecture is BERT, declared in the config as BertForMaskedLM with 30 hidden layers, a hidden size of 1024, 16 attention heads, an intermediate size of 4096 and a vocabulary of 30 tokens. Unlike the original BERT there is no next-sentence prediction, because each protein sequence is treated as a complete document. Masking follows the original recipe: 15 per cent of amino acids are chosen, 80 per cent of those are replaced by the mask token, 10 per cent by a different random amino acid and 10 per cent left as they are. Sequences are uppercased and split with single spaces, and the rare letters U, Z, O and B are mapped to X. Training ran on one TPU Pod V3-512 for 400,000 steps, 300,000 at sequence length 512 with batch size 15k and 100,000 at length 2048 with batch size 2.5k, with the Lamb optimiser at learning rate 0.002.
sections.source_locator: config.json; model card Model description, Preprocessing and Pretraining

sections.title: Versions and reproducibility
sections.body: Two BERT checkpoints exist in the ProtTrans family and they differ in their training corpus: ProtBert, trained on UniRef100, and ProtBert-BFD, trained on BFD. The paper gives both the same 30-layer architecture; ProtBert was trained for 300k steps at length 512 and 100k at length 2048, ProtBert-BFD for 800k and then 200k steps at the same two lengths. A result should say which one, since the ProtTrans README reports different downstream numbers for them, for example 75 against 76 on CASP12 three-state secondary structure. Each is published both on the Hugging Face hub and on Zenodo, and neither is gated. The Hugging Face revisions read here are 7a894481acdc12202f0a415dd567f6cfdb698908 for ProtBert and 6c5c8a55a52ff08a664dfd584aa1773f125a0487 for ProtBert-BFD. The wider ProtTrans release also holds ProtT5, ProtAlbert, ProtXLNet and ProtElectra models, which are different architectures and not covered here.
sections.source_locator: ProtTrans README Models Availability and the secondary structure tables; Hugging Face API responses for both checkpoints

sections.title: Licensing: code and weights differ
sections.body: The ProtTrans repository code is MIT. The pretrained models are not: the README states they are released under the Academic Free License v3.0. The Hugging Face repository for ProtBert declares no licence at all in its card metadata, so the README is the only statement of terms for the weights. Anyone redistributing or building a product on the weights should read the Academic Free License itself rather than assume the repository's MIT terms apply to them.

profile.summary: DeepFoldRNA predicts the 3D (tertiary) structure of an RNA from its sequence alone. It builds a multiple sequence alignment and secondary structure prediction for the input RNA, uses a deep self-attention network to predict distance and angle restraints, and then folds the chain by gradient-based simulation. The output is all-atom models in PDB format, before and after refinement.
profile.summary_source_locator: bioRxiv abstract; README.txt: Running instructions

sections.title: How it works
sections.body: The pipeline has four stages. First, rMSA builds an MSA and PETfold predicts secondary structure; SPOT-RNA-1D predicts torsion angles. Second, a neural network with 48 MSA transformer blocks, 4 single-sequence blocks and 2 pair blocks, run for 4 recycling cycles, predicts restraints: binned distances from 2 to 40 Angstrom, inter-residue orientation angles and torsion angles. The paper trained it with a cross-entropy loss on binned restraints plus a BERT-style loss on masked MSA positions, using Adam at learning rate 0.001 on a single V100 GPU. Third, gradient-based folding simulations build the structure from these restraints. Fourth, SimRNA and QRNAS refine the full-atom model. The authors note that the restraints do not include base atoms, so the unrefined model has slightly better backbone RMSD but worse base pairing than the refined one.
sections.source_locator: README.txt; network/config.py; paper Methods

sections.title: Versions and reproducibility
sections.body: The stand-alone program is Version 1.0, dated 03/28/2022. The network weights are stored in the repository under network/parameters, in four folders (model_1, model_1_2, model_2, model_2_2) of three weight files each. By default the program makes 6 models with different network parameters, or 3 if --generate_all_models is False. Results also depend on the sequence databases used for MSA generation. A result should name the commit (this page read 0c2c1925), the model number and whether the refined or unrefined model was used. A web server is also available.

strengths.text: Needs only the RNA sequence as input; the MSA and secondary structure are generated by the pipeline.
The authors report an average RMSD of 2.69 Angstrom and TM-score of 0.743 on Rfam and RNA-Puzzles benchmarks, and about 1 minute to fold a medium-sized RNA. These are the authors' own figures.
Each stage can be run on its own (input generation, restraint prediction, folding, refinement), which helps reuse of precomputed MSAs.

limitations.text: The sequence databases for MSA generation need more than 500 GB of disk and hours to download; the program needs an x86_64 Linux machine.
Non-commercial licence per the README, with a conflicting MIT LICENSE file; several third-party tools (PETfold, rMSA, SimRNA, QRNAS, SPOT-RNA-1D) have their own licences.
The unrefined model has worse base pairing because the restraints do not cover base atoms, and refinement can introduce chain breaks.

Single-chain RNA only, with standard bases A, G, C and U; the sources describe no complexes or modified nucleotides, and the authors list extension to RNA complexes and RNA-protein interactions as future work.

profile.summary: Orthrus is a family of RNA foundation models that turn a full mature mRNA transcript into an embedding. It was pretrained so that splice isoforms of the same gene, and transcripts of orthologous genes across mammals, get similar embeddings. The embeddings are used, directly or after fine-tuning, to predict mRNA properties such as RNA half-life and ribosome load.
profile.summary_source_locator: Preprint abstract; README: Model Overview

sections.title: How it works
sections.body: Orthrus uses a Mamba encoder, a state-space model whose memory grows linearly with sequence length, so it can read whole mRNAs. The input is a per-base track matrix: four one-hot nucleotide tracks, plus in the 6-track models a coding sequence track (1 at the first base of each codon) and a splice track (1 at the last base of each exon). Pretraining is contrastive: pairs of transcripts formed from splice isoforms and orthologues pass through the encoder and a projection head, and a decoupled contrastive learning loss pulls each pair together; the projection head is then discarded. One released checkpoint adds a masked language modelling objective. The paper trained all models with Adam for 20,000 steps, on four A100 or H100 GPUs, except Orthrus Small, which used A40 and L40 GPUs. The model returns a mean-pooled embedding per transcript, or per-position hidden states.
sections.source_locator: README; model cards; paper Orthrus Model Overview and Appendix A.3

Three pre-publication checkpoints sit under quietflamingo. The GitHub README still describes the earlier 4-track base and 6-track large models loaded from local Lightning checkpoint files. steps.title: Load the model and embed a sequence
steps.shell:
python - <<'PY'
import torch
from transformers import AutoModel

device = torch.device("cuda" if torch.cuda.is_available() else "cpu")

model = AutoModel.from_pretrained(
    "antichronology/orthrus-4-track",
    trust_remote_code=True,
).to(device).eval()

sequence = (
    "TCATCTGGATTATACATATTTCGCAATGAAAGAGAGGAAGAAAAGGAAGCAGCAAAATATGTGGAGGCCCA"
    "ACAAAAGAGACTAGAAGCCTTATTCACTAAAATTCAGGAGGAATTTGAAGAACATGAAGTTACTTCCTCC"
)
oh = model.seq_to_oh(sequence).unsqueeze(0).to(device)  # (1, L, 4)
lengths = torch.tensor([oh.shape[1]], device=device)

with torch.no_grad():
    emb = model.representation(oh, lengths, channel_last=True)
# emb.shape == (1, D)
PY
steps.explanation: The model card's load and pooled-representation snippets, joined and wrapped in a shell heredoc. It downloads the weights and runs custom model code from the Hugging Face repository (trust_remote_code).

profile.summary: DGRNA is a pretrained RNA language model built for long RNA sequences. It is built mainly from bidirectional Mamba2 layers rather than the Transformer layers of earlier RNA language models, a choice the authors make to handle long sequences efficiently, and was trained on about 100 million RNA sequences from the MARS database. Given RNA sequences, the released code returns a per-position representation that can be used for downstream tasks.
profile.summary_source_locator: README: About; bioRxiv abstract; DGRNA/mamba2_pretrained.py: MambaLMHeadModel.forward

sections.title: How it works
sections.body: Tokens are embedded and passed through pairs of Mamba2 blocks: one reads the sequence forwards and one reads it reversed. A linear layer merges each pair's outputs. After the last pair, one multi-head attention layer with 32 heads and rotary embeddings is applied, followed by a final normalisation. The paper describes 12 bidirectional Mamba2 blocks, an output embedding of 768 dimensions per position and 100 million parameters. Pretraining is masked language modelling as in BERT: 15% of nucleotide tokens are corrupted and the model learns to recover them. Sequences are tokenised one nucleotide at a time, with T replaced by U and [CLS] and [EOS] tokens added at the ends. The model is built on the ESM and Fairseq code bases and uses an ESM-1b style alphabet. The released forward pass returns the hidden states, not token logits.

strengths.text: The authors chose Mamba layers to avoid the quadratic cost of Transformer attention, so the design targets long RNA sequences.
Each layer reads the sequence in both directions, so every position's representation uses context on both sides.
The authors report in the preprint abstract that DGRNA performed better than existing RNA language models on six downstream tasks.

The README lists dependency versions but gives no install command.
At 100 million parameters, DGRNA is smaller than most RNA language models, as the authors themselves note.

profile.summary: ProtRNA is an RNA language model made by adapting a protein language model, ESM-2, to RNA sequences. The authors' idea is that information learned from the much larger body of protein sequences can transfer to RNA, where sequences are fewer and less conserved. It takes RNA sequences and returns per-nucleotide embeddings, which the repository uses for secondary structure, protein-RNA interaction and mean ribosome loading prediction.
profile.summary_source_locator: README: Abstract, Inference, Evaluation; bioRxiv abstract

sections.title: How it works
sections.body: ProtRNA starts from the 650M-parameter ESM-2 protein language model and is trained further on RNA by a cross-modality transfer learning strategy. The first 29 of its 33 transformer layers stay frozen; only the last four layers and the embeddings for the new RNA tokens are trained. Training is masked language modelling as in RoBERTa, with 15% of tokens as targets, on 6 million representative non-coding RNA sequences from RNAcentral, for six epochs. The model keeps the ESM-2 vocabulary of amino acids and appends lower-case RNA tokens (a, u, g, c, x), so the same alphabet holds both kinds of sequence. Input RNA is lower-cased, T is mapped to u, and any other character becomes x. The pretrained model built by the loader has 33 layers, embedding dimension 1280 and 20 attention heads. Embeddings from layer 33 feed separate prediction heads for each downstream task; in the paper only the heads are trained and the language model is not fine-tuned.

sections.body: One pretrained language model is released, ProtRNA_pretrained.h5, as TensorFlow weights on Zenodo record 14795554. The same record holds task heads: four RotaFormer secondary structure heads trained on different datasets and selected under different metrics, protein-RNA interaction heads for 17 RBPs in HeLa cells, and a mean ribosome loading head (the last two in PyTorch). The README notes that an earlier version of the paper scored secondary structure with the authors' own metrics and keeps a script for that. A result should name the Zenodo record, the head file and the repository commit; this page read commit 991037d6. The preprint has two bioRxiv versions, and the bioRxiv record links a published version, DOI 10.1016/j.cels.2025.101371.

strengths.text: The authors report comparable or better results than RNA language models on several downstream tasks while using 1/8 the trainable parameters and 1/6 the training data of the primary baseline, RiNALMo. This is the authors' claim.
Weights, trained task heads and the downstream datasets are all released together, with scripts to re-run the secondary structure, RBP and mean ribosome loading evaluations.
Base inference needs only numpy and TensorFlow. Code is Apache-2.0 and weights are CC BY 4.0.

limitations.text: The model is TensorFlow only, while two of the task heads are PyTorch, so the downstream pipelines need both frameworks.
Sequences longer than 512 tokens are cut by the default batch converter, and 512 was the pretraining context. The paper reports secondary structure F1 falling as sequence length grows.
The pretrained weights file is large, 2,605,079,184 bytes, and is fetched with wget on first use.

The authors report that the uneven mix of RNA families in the training data shows in the results: secondary structure prediction is best for 5S rRNA and tRNA, which are common in the data, and worst for telomerase RNA, which makes up 0.01%.

profile.summary: Uni-RNA is a pre-trained language model for RNA sequences from DP Technology. Its pre-training database holds about 1 billion RNA sequences. The paper's Table 8 lists 100M training sequences for its L8 and L12 models and 500M for L16 and L24, while its Discussion says Uni-RNA was trained on one billion sequences; the files read do not confirm that the released checkpoints are the models in Table 8. It reads an RNA sequence and returns a learned representation (embedding) for each position, or predicted probabilities for masked positions. The authors fine-tune these representations for RNA structure and function prediction tasks.
profile.summary_source_locator: bioRxiv abstract; README.md: Model summary and Quick Start; paper: Methods, Table 8, Discussion

sections.title: How it works
sections.body: Uni-RNA is a BERT-style encoder-only Transformer with a masked-language-model head: the masked-LM class outputs, for each position, logits over the token vocabulary. The paper pre-trains it by masked nucleic acid modelling, with a training strategy similar to BERT; it does not give the masking rate. The released configurations use 64-dimensional attention heads, a GELU feed-forward layer three times the hidden size, rotary position embeddings and a vocabulary of 10 tokens; in the L16 upload these are four special tokens (<pad>, <eos>, <cls>, <mask>) and the letters N, A, T, C, G and U. In training, the paper converts U to T, uses N for rare bases and adds start and end tokens. The last hidden layer gives per-position embeddings that can be used directly, with a linear probe, or fine-tuned for a downstream task; the paper reports that fine-tuning does better than linear probing.
sections.source_locator: README.md: Model summary; hf-vocab-L16.txt; paper: Figure 1 legend, Methods 4.2 Model and 4.4 Downstream Tasks

sections.title: Versions and reproducibility
sections.body: Three checkpoints are released: L8 (8 layers, hidden size 512), L12 (12 layers, hidden size 768) and L16 (16 layers, hidden size 1024). The paper also describes a larger L24 model (24 layers, embedding size 1280, 400M parameters), used for its secondary structure results; the README does not list L24 among the released checkpoints. The repository distributes the three together as one weights archive on Google Drive, with no version label. Uploads named UniRNA-L8, UniRNA-L12 and UniRNA-L16 also exist on Hugging Face under the EscheWang account, but the repository README does not link to them. A result should name the checkpoint (L8, L12 or L16) and where the weights came from.

profile.summary: DeepVariant is a germline variant caller: it finds SNPs and small indels in a person's sequencing reads. It takes reads aligned to a reference genome, turns the reads around each candidate site into a pileup image, classifies that image with a convolutional neural network, and writes the calls to a VCF or gVCF file. Trained models are provided for short-read, long-read and other sequencing technologies, all trained on human data.
profile.summary_source_locator: README.md: introduction and notes; paper title

sections.title: How it works
sections.body: DeepVariant runs as three programs. make_examples reads the aligned reads and the reference, finds candidate variant sites with high sensitivity but low specificity, and writes a multi-channel tensor for each candidate site. All models use six base channels (read base, base quality, mapping quality, strand, whether the read supports the allele, and whether the base matches the reference); Illumina models add an insert size channel and PacBio and ONT models add a haplotype channel. call_variants classifies each tensor with a convolutional network into the three diploid genotypes, and is the only step that uses a GPU. The network is trained on reads from samples whose true genotypes are known. postprocess_variants sorts the results, combines multi-allelic records and writes a VCF, and optionally a gVCF. Genotypes are limited to hom-ref, het and hom-alt. The paper describes the version that entered the 2016 precisionFDA challenge, which used the Inception-v2 architecture on three-channel RGB pileup images; the paper and the usage guide both say the open-source rewrite moved to Inception-v3 and multichannel tensors. The sources read do not state the architecture of the v1.10 models.
sections.source_locator: usage guide; paper: Main Text, Limitations and Online methods

sections.title: Versions and reproducibility
sections.body: DeepVariant is released as numbered versions; the README read is for v1.10, with Docker image google/deepvariant:1.10.0. Each release bundles its models inside the Docker image, selected with --model_type: WGS, WES, PACBIO, ONT_R104 or HYBRID_PACBIO_ILLUMINA. Model files for all releases are also kept in a public Google Cloud bucket. Training data change between releases, so a result must name the release version and the model type. The paper's results are for the 2016 challenge version and for GitHub v0.4.1, not for v1.10.

strengths.text: Training data per release and model type are documented sample by sample.

The authors report that a model trained on human data generalises across genome builds and to other mammals: a model trained on GRCh37 reads scored F1 = 99.45% on GRCh38 reads, and a human-trained model scored F1 = 98.29% on mouse data. These are the paper's figures for its 2016 version.

The included models are trained on human data only; the developers point to pitfalls for other organisms.

Memory can be large in the last step: postprocess_variants may need 2 to 3 GB per core, or 20 to 50 GB in total when run single-threaded.

run_guide.summary: Pull the DeepVariant 1.10.0 Docker image, download the small test bundle and call variants in a 10 kb region of chromosome 20.
prerequisites: A Unix-like machine with the AVX instruction set and Docker (the quick start installs docker.io with apt).
No GPU needed; a GPU image exists for the call_variants step.
Network access to Docker Hub and storage.googleapis.com.
Code is BSD-3-Clause; no separate licence for the models is stated.

steps.title: Get the Docker image
steps.shell:
BIN_VERSION="1.10.0"

sudo apt -y update
sudo apt-get -y install docker.io
sudo docker pull google/deepvariant:"${BIN_VERSION}"
steps.explanation: Copied from the quick start. The models are inside the image.

steps.title: Download the test bundle
steps.shell:
INPUT_DIR="${PWD}/quickstart-testdata"
DATA_HTTP_DIR="https://storage.googleapis.com/deepvariant/quickstart-testdata"

mkdir -p ${INPUT_DIR}
wget -P ${INPUT_DIR} "${DATA_HTTP_DIR}"/NA12878_S1.chr20.10_10p1mb.bam
wget -P ${INPUT_DIR} "${DATA_HTTP_DIR}"/NA12878_S1.chr20.10_10p1mb.bam.bai
wget -P ${INPUT_DIR} "${DATA_HTTP_DIR}"/ucsc.hg19.chr20.unittest.fasta
wget -P ${INPUT_DIR} "${DATA_HTTP_DIR}"/ucsc.hg19.chr20.unittest.fasta.fai
steps.explanation: A subset of the quick start's download lines: the BAM, its index, the reference FASTA and its index, which the run step uses. The quick start also downloads truth files for evaluation with hap.py.

steps.title: Call variants
steps.shell:
OUTPUT_DIR="${PWD}/quickstart-output"
mkdir -p "${OUTPUT_DIR}"

sudo docker run \
  -v "${INPUT_DIR}":"/input" \
  -v "${OUTPUT_DIR}":"/output" \
  google/deepvariant:"${BIN_VERSION}" \
  /opt/deepvariant/bin/run_deepvariant \
  --model_type=WGS \
  --vcf_stats_report=true \
  --ref=/input/ucsc.hg19.chr20.unittest.fasta \
  --reads=/input/NA12878_S1.chr20.10_10p1mb.bam \
  --regions "chr20:10,000,000-10,010,000" \
  --output_vcf=/output/output.vcf.gz \
  --output_gvcf=/output/output.g.vcf.gz \
  --intermediate_results_dir /output/intermediate_results_dir \
  --num_shards=1
steps.explanation: Copied from the quick start. run_deepvariant runs make_examples, call_variants and postprocess_variants in turn.
steps.source_locator: deepvariant-quick-start.md: Run DeepVariant with one command

outputs: In quickstart-output: output.vcf.gz and output.g.vcf.gz with their .tbi indexes, output.visual_report.html, and the intermediate_results_dir directory.
limitations: These commands were read from the repository and have not been executed by Rewire.
The example covers 10 kb of chromosome 20 with the WGS model; other data types need a different --model_type.
The test data are on hg19; this says nothing about accuracy on other builds.

profile.summary: ModernGENA is a DNA language model that adapts the ModernBERT encoder to genomic sequences. It reads DNA split into byte-pair-encoding (BPE) tokens and was pretrained by masked language modelling on 443 vertebrate genome assemblies. It outputs token embeddings that are fine-tuned for downstream tasks such as sequence classification or per-token regression; the authors present it as an efficient baseline for future DNA model work.
profile.summary_source_locator: Europe PMC abstract; model card: Tokenization, Pretraining corpus; GENA_LM examples README

sections.title: How it works
sections.body: ModernGENA is a BERT-style encoder built on ModernBERT. The model card and the paper list RoPE positional embeddings, hybrid local and global attention, pre-norm transformer blocks, GeGLU feed-forward layers and end-to-end unpadding, with FlashAttention for faster inference on compatible hardware. In the published configurations, local attention covers 128 tokens and every third layer uses global attention. Input DNA is tokenised with the 32k BPE vocabulary from GENA-LM over the symbols A, T, G, C and N; long runs of N are collapsed into one token. Pretraining used masked language modelling on intervals sampled from -16 kbp to +8 kbp around each transcription start site, on both strands, to reduce the weight of simple repeats. Training sequences were packed with lengths drawn between 10 and 1024 tokens. Whole chromosomes were held out for validation; for human these were chromosomes 8, 20 and 21.
sections.source_locator: model card; config.json; paper: sections 3.1 Architecture, 3.2 Training

sections.title: Versions and reproducibility
sections.body: Two checkpoints are released on Hugging Face: ModernGENA base (22 layers, hidden size 768, 12 attention heads) and ModernGENA large (28 layers, hidden size 1024, 16 attention heads). Both use the same tokenizer, the same pretraining corpus and a vocabulary of 32768 tokens. The base model card states 377M parameters, which is the large model's figure; the paper gives 135M for base. A result should name the checkpoint and its Hugging Face revision; this page read base at revision 7036ebb6 and large at revision 01de8202. The paper says the full implementation and configuration are released, and that the training and fine-tuning code is in the GENA_LM repository.
sections.source_locator: config.json of both checkpoints; Hugging Face API responses, sha; Europe PMC abstract; model card

facts.label: Model type
facts.value: BERT-style DNA foundation model (encoder) pretrained with masked language modelling.
facts.source_locator: Model card: introduction and tags; config.json architectures

facts.label: Architecture
facts.value: ModernBERT encoder with RoPE positional embeddings, hybrid local/global attention (local window 128, global attention every 3 layers), pre-norm blocks and GeGLU feed-forward layers, with bias terms disabled in most linear and LayerNorm layers. Base: 22 layers, hidden size 768, intermediate size 1152. Large: 28 layers, hidden size 1024, intermediate size 2624. The paper uses FlashAttention v3 for global layers and v2 for local layers. The released config.json files set position_embedding_type to absolute, while the paper and the card say RoPE.
facts.source_locator: model card; config.json of both checkpoints; paper: section 3.1 and Appendix A, Table 1

facts.label: Inputs
facts.value: DNA sequence over A/T/G/C/N, tokenised with the GENA-LM 32k BPE tokenizer (AIRI-Institute/gena-lm-bert-base-t2t), with special tokens [CLS], [SEP], [PAD], [UNK] and [MASK].
facts.source_locator: Model card: Tokenization; Load pretrained model

facts.label: Outputs
facts.value: Per-token hidden states from the encoder, used as a starting point for fine-tuning. The linked examples fine-tune it for sequence classification and per-token regression.
facts.source_locator: Model card: Load pretrained model; GENA_LM examples README

facts.label: Parameters
facts.value: ModernGENA base: 136,120,832. ModernGENA large: 377,841,664. Counted by Hugging Face from the published safetensors files. The paper gives 135M (base) and 377M (large). The base model card says 377M, which matches the large checkpoint, not the base file.
facts.source_locator: Hugging Face API responses, safetensors; model card introduction; paper: section 3.1 and Appendix A

facts.label: Training data
facts.value: 443 vertebrate genome assemblies, 353,574,093,776 bp in total: all vertebrate species with genome and transcript annotations in NCBI RefSeq as of December 2024. Forward and reverse complement strands, excluding sequences with symbols other than A/C/G/T. Training intervals were sampled from -16 kbp to +8 kbp around transcription start sites. ModernGENA base processed 1,510B tokens over 158 epochs and large 1,320B tokens over 138 epochs.

profile.summary: SpliceAI2 is a deep learning model from Illumina that predicts RNA splicing from genomic sequence. It reads about 200 kb of DNA around a gene and predicts how much each position is used as a splice donor or acceptor, how much each splice junction is used, and the most likely complete transcripts. Comparing predictions for reference and alternate alleles gives a score for how strongly a variant changes splicing.
profile.summary_source_locator: Manuscript: Main 'Hierarchical model of RNA splicing'; Methods 'Variant effect prediction'; README: introduction

sections.title: How it works
sections.body: The input is 196,608 bp of genomic sequence on the gene's sense strand, one-hot encoded, plus a one-hot code for the species (ten channels). A dense layer projects it to 256 channels, and 20 MetaFormer blocks follow, each with a depth-wise dilated convolution and a feed-forward network, at progressively coarser pooling. Each block's output feeds a splice site head over the central 65,536 positions. The 1,024 positions with the highest splice site usage are then paired by a query-key product to give a 1,024 by 1,024 matrix of splice junction usage. Sites and junctions form a splice graph, and Viterbi decoding finds the highest scoring paths, which are the predicted transcripts. The model was trained end-to-end on splice site, junction and transcript usage, with the three losses summed.
sections.source_locator: Manuscript: Methods 'SpliceAI2 model' (Inputs, Architecture, Outputs, Training); 'Transcript prediction'

sections.title: Versions and reproducibility
sections.body: The code is package version 2.0 (this page read commit 1dcd2a18 on main). The released model is an ensemble of two checkpoints trained with identical settings, held on Hugging Face as spliceai2_multispecies_13M_01 and spliceai2_multispecies_13M_02, each with a model.ckpt; the README's commands pass both folders. Illumina also publishes precomputed scores for all possible single nucleotide variants and observed indels in protein-coding genes (GENCODE v48, GRCh38). The manuscript also describes a tissue-specific model conditioned on RBP expression; the files read do not show it as released. A result should name the package version, both checkpoint folders and the Hugging Face revision (55948bae read here).
sections.source_locator: setup.py; Hugging Face file listing; manuscript: Methods 'Training', Extended Data Fig. 3; README

facts.label: Model type
facts.value: Supervised sequence-to-function model for splicing: predicts splice site, splice junction and transcript usage, and scores variant effects on splicing.
facts.source_locator: Manuscript: Abstract; README: introduction

facts.label: Architecture
facts.value: A dense input projection to 256 channels, then 20 MetaFormer blocks (depth-wise dilated convolution token mixer, feed-forward channel mixer) with multi-scale pooling; per-block splice site heads; a query-key junction head with rotary position embeddings over the top 1,024 sites; Viterbi decoding of a splice graph for transcripts. PyTorch Lightning implementation.
facts.source_locator: Manuscript: Methods 'SpliceAI2 model'; setup.py

facts.label: Inputs
facts.value: For the model: 196,608 bp of genomic sequence on the gene's sense strand, one-hot encoded, plus species identity. For the scoring tool: a TSV of variants (chrom, pos, ref, alt, strand) and a reference genome FASTA.
facts.source_locator: Manuscript: Methods 'Inputs'; README: Variant effect prediction

facts.label: Outputs
facts.value: Splice donor and acceptor usage over the central 65,536 positions, junction usage for pairs among 1,024 candidate sites, and top-k transcripts. The scoring tool writes a spliceai2_summary_score from 0 to 1 plus 260 detail columns; recommended thresholds are 0.1 (high recall), 0.25 (balance) and 0.5 (high precision).
facts.source_locator: Manuscript: Methods 'Outputs'; README: Variant effect prediction

facts.label: Parameters
facts.value: Approximately 13 million trainable parameters per model, as stated in the manuscript; the released ensemble has two such models. Each model.ckpt file is 117,134,011 bytes (folder _01).
facts.source_locator: Manuscript: Methods 'Architecture'; Hugging Face listing of spliceai2_multispecies_13M_01

facts.label: Training data
facts.value: Splice junctions from 314,745 bulk short-read RNA-seq samples (67,493,026 junctions) in ten mammalian species, from recount3 and the NCBI SRA, restricted to protein-coding genes; plus transcripts from 330 ENCODE long-read RNA-seq samples (189 human, 141 mouse). Genes on human chromosomes 21 and 22 were held out for validation.
facts.source_locator: Manuscript: Methods 'Training datasets' and 'Training'

facts.label: Known versions
facts.value: SpliceAI2 2.0: an ensemble of two checkpoints, spliceai2_multispecies_13M_01 and spliceai2_multispecies_13M_02, on Hugging Face (read at revision 55948bae). Precomputed scores are also distributed. It is the successor of SpliceAI, and the README maps SpliceAI thresholds and output columns to SpliceAI2 ones.
facts.source_locator: setup.py; Hugging Face listing; README

facts.label: Training cutoff
facts.value: Not reported. The manuscript names the datasets (recount3, SRA, ENCODE long-read) but gives no download date.
facts.source_locator: Manuscript: Methods 'Training datasets'

facts.label: Context limits
facts.value: Trained on inputs of 196,608 bp; predictions cover the central 65,536 positions and junctions among the top 1,024 sites. The README's transcript example uses L + 131,072 nt of input with L a multiple of 16, predicting the central L positions.
facts.source_locator: Manuscript: Methods 'Inputs', 'Outputs'; README: Transcript prediction

facts.label: Code licence
facts.value: The same SpliceAI2 Model Terms of Use: the terms define SpliceAI2 to include its source code. Not an open-source licence.
facts.source_locator: LICENSE section 1(f); setup.py

facts.label: Access
facts.value: Code: https://github.com/Illumina/SpliceAI2 and PyPI (pip install spliceai2). Weights and precomputed scores: https://huggingface.co/illumina-ai/SpliceAI2, gated; access requires accepting the terms and giving a printed name, academic affiliation and academic email. strengths.text: It predicts splice junctions and whole transcripts as well as splice sites, so a variant's effect can be read as a change in transcript structure, not only a site score.
Long context: each prediction sees 196,608 bp of sequence.
Precomputed scores cover all possible single nucleotide variants and observed indels in human protein-coding genes, and the output keeps SpliceAI-compatible columns and threshold equivalents.
The authors report improved detection of splice-altering variants and better quantification of their effects across cryptic splicing, sQTL and MPRA benchmarks; this is their claim.

limitations.text: Restrictive licence: non-commercial organisations only, no redistribution, no use to train other models, research use only and not for diagnostic procedures. This applies to the code as well as the weights. The weights are also gated on Hugging Face and need a manual access request with academic details.
limitations.source_locator: LICENSE: preamble, sections 1(f), 3 and 13; Hugging Face API gated, extra_gated_fields

limitations.text: A CUDA-capable GPU is required.
The user must supply the gene strand for each variant; if it is unknown, both strands have to be scored and combined.

The released model takes only sequence and species as input. The authors state that predicting how splice-altering effects vary across tissues, cell types and developmental contexts still needs further work.

profile.summary: GPN-Promoter (Hugging Face name gpn-animal-promoter) is a DNA language model trained on 512-bp promoter windows from 434 animal genomes. It was released with TraitGym, a benchmark of causal regulatory variants in human genetics. Given a DNA window, it predicts masked nucleotides; the GPN tools turn this into a variant score, the log-likelihood ratio of the alternate against the reference allele, or into sequence embeddings.

sections.title: How it works
sections.body: GPN-Promoter belongs to the GPN (GPN-SS) family: single-sequence genomic language models trained on unaligned genomes with masked language modelling. The paper trains it on 512-bp windows centred on the transcription start sites of protein-coding genes, with base-pair tokens and repeat positions (soft-masked in the reference genome) down-weighted to 0.01. The architecture follows ByteNet: blocks that alternate dilated convolutions and feed-forward layers. The published config has 64 layers and hidden size 1024, a first kernel size of 9 and later kernel size of 5, with dilation base 2 cycling every 8 layers. The vocabulary has 7 tokens, from the tokenizer gonzalobenegas/tokenizer-dna-mlm named in the training script. Training ran 370K steps at batch size 2048, which took about 2 weeks on 4 NVIDIA A100 40GB GPUs. For variant scoring, the GPN package compares the model's likelihood of the alternate and reference alleles, averaged over both strands.

sections.title: Versions and reproducibility
sections.body: One model is published, songlab/gpn-animal-promoter, read here at revision 7cf3276a. Intermediate training checkpoints from the same run are in a separate Hugging Face dataset, and the training data are in songlab/gpn-animal-promoter-dataset. The analysis code that produced the model is preserved under the ref analysis-archive-2026-08-18 of the GPN repository. The model card imports gpn.model, while the current GPN docs (commit dc5fd287 read here) load GPN models through register_auto_classes("ss"). A result should name the Hugging Face revision and the GPN package version used to load it.

profile.summary: CARP is a family of protein language models built from convolutions rather than attention. Each model reads an amino acid sequence and was pretrained to fill in masked residues, on the March 2020 release of UniRef50. It returns a representation for every residue, plus per-residue logits that can be used to score sequences. Because it is a convolutional network, cost grows linearly with length rather than quadratically.
profile.summary_source_locator: README: Convolutional autoencoding representations of proteins (CARP); abstract

sections.title: How it works
sections.body: Each CARP model is a ByteNet encoder: stacked convolutional layers with growing dilation, so a residue's representation takes in a widening window of neighbours without attention. In the paper, an embedding layer maps each token to 8 dimensions, a linear layer maps that to the model width, and a stack of ByteNet blocks with 1 x 5 dilated convolutions follows, with the dilation rate doubling each layer up to 128 and then restarting at 1; a final layer norm gives the representation and a linear decoder gives the logits. Pretraining selects 15% of residues, replaces 80% of them with a mask token, 10% with a random amino acid and leaves 10% unchanged, and asks the model to recover them, as in ESM-1b. The loader reads the width, depth, kernel size and dilation factor from the checkpoint and builds a ByteNetLM over the protein alphabet, then wraps it so padding is masked. Forward returns per-residue representations; with repr_layers and logits you also get intermediate layers and the vocabulary logits.
sections.source_locator: README; sequence_models/pretrained.py; paper: Method Details (Architecture; Dataset and Masked Language Modeling)

sections.body: Four sizes are released and are chosen by name in load_model_and_alphabet: carp_600k, carp_38M, carp_76M and carp_640M. The paper trained seven sizes, from CARP-4k to CARP-640M; The README lists only the four released names; CARP-4k, CARP-40k and CARP-24M are not among them. The loader fetches each released model from one Zenodo deposit, so a result should name the checkpoint and that deposit (record 6564798, dated 2022-03-18). The same loader also serves MIF, MIF-ST and BiGCARP from other deposits; MIF-ST pulls carp_640M in as its sequence model, so a MIF-ST result is not a CARP result.

facts.label: Architecture
facts.value: ByteNet encoder: stacked dilated convolutional layers with 1 x 5 kernels, dilation doubling up to 128 and repeating, then a final layer norm and a linear decoder. The loader builds a ByteNetLM with the embedding size, model width, layer count, kernel size and dilation factor stored in each checkpoint, with final layer normalisation and no causal masking. Per the paper's Table S1: CARP-600k 16 layers, d 128; CARP-38M 16 layers, d 1024; CARP-76M 32 layers, d 1024; CARP-640M 56 layers, d 1280.

The authors note that, without attention, CARP lacks the attention maps that transformers offer for reading out contacts or binding sites. They also found that more masked-language pretraining did not reliably help out-of-domain protein engineering tasks.

profile.summary: EVE (evolutionary model of variant effect) predicts whether a single amino acid change in a human protein is likely to cause disease, without training on clinical labels. For each protein it learns from a multiple sequence alignment of that protein's family across organisms. The output is a score per missense variant giving the probability that it falls in the pathogenic cluster, with an uncertainty on that assignment.
profile.summary_source_locator: Paper abstract; README: Overview, Data requirements

sections.title: How it works
sections.body: EVE has three steps. First, a Bayesian variational autoencoder (VAE) is trained on a re-weighted multiple sequence alignment for one protein family and learns a distribution over its sequences; each sequence is down-weighted by the number of neighbours within a Hamming distance of 0.2, to correct for sampling and phylogenetic bias. Second, the trained VAE gives each single amino acid mutation an evolutionary index, the difference in evidence lower bound (ELBO) between mutant and wild type, which approximates the log-likelihood ratio. Third, a global-local mixture of Gaussian mixture models splits the variants into a benign and a pathogenic cluster on that index: a two-component GMM fitted on all proteins is mixed with a per-protein GMM, the per-protein one weighted 0.3. The EVE score is the probabilistic assignment to the pathogenic cluster, and its predictive entropy gives the uncertainty. In the default settings the encoder has hidden layers of 2000, 1000 and 300 units, the latent space has 50 dimensions, and the decoder is Bayesian.
sections.source_locator: README; default_model_params.json; paper: Methods (Training VAEs over Multiple Sequence Alignments; Evolutionary index; Separating pathogenic and benign variants)

sections.title: Alignments and precomputed scores
sections.body: The developers built each alignment with five Jackhmmer iterations against UniRef100 (downloaded on 20 April 2020), using EVcouplings, kept sequences covering at least 50% of the target and columns with at least 70% occupancy, and chose a bit score threshold per protein to balance coverage and depth. The README reports training data for 3,219 clinically relevant proteins, and the journal abstract reports predictions for more than 36 million variants across 3,219 disease genes. The bioRxiv preprint (version 1) reports an earlier set: 1,081 proteins and 11 million variants. Precomputed EVE scores, alignments and ClinVar labels for all proteins are offered on evemodel.org; the repository itself ships alignments and labels for four proteins (P53, PTEN, RASH and SCN5A).

sections.title: Versions and reproducibility
sections.body: EVE is a method, not one pretrained network: a separate VAE is trained for each protein, and the repository releases no trained VAE weights. A result should name the code commit, the alignment used (its bit score threshold and preprocessing), the VAE settings file, the number of samples used for the evolutionary index (20000 in the example script; the preprint used 200k) and the GMM parameters (the repository ships default GMM parameters). This page read the repository at commit 460d70ef.

strengths.text: Trains without disease labels, so its scores are not shaped by the sparse and biased labels the authors say limit supervised predictors.
Precomputed scores for all single amino acid mutations in thousands of proteins can be downloaded, so many users need not train anything.
Code is MIT licensed and the repository includes example scripts, alignments and ClinVar labels to reproduce scores for PTEN end to end.

The developers' claim, from the paper: EVE outperforms computational approaches trained on labelled data and performs on par with high-throughput experiments. In the preprint, EVE scores reach an aggregate AUC of 0.90 against ClinVar labels across 1,081 proteins, 0.93 when the 25% most uncertain variants are set aside.

limitations.text: Needs a good multiple sequence alignment for every protein, and a separate VAE is trained for each one. The authors expect performance to depend on alignment quality.

limitations.text: Scores single amino acid substitutions only; the sources read describe no support for insertions, deletions or multiple mutations in the scoring pipeline, and the preprint says combinations of variants were not explored.

Training is long by default (400000 steps per protein), and the environment pins older software: python 3.7, pytorch 1.7 and cudatoolkit 11.0. GPU type and memory are not stated. The authors avoided very large genes such as TTN because of the compute needed.
No trained model weights are released; only code, four example alignments and the precomputed scores on evemodel.org.

profile.summary: ProSST is a protein language model that reads both a protein's amino acid sequence and its 3D structure. The structure is first converted into a sequence of discrete structure tokens, one per residue, and the model is pretrained to predict masked residues. Its main use in the repository is zero-shot prediction of the effect of amino acid substitutions, scored on the ProteinGym benchmark.
profile.summary_source_locator: Abstract; README: 4 Zero-shot mutant effect prediction

sections.title: How it works
sections.body: ProSST has two parts. The structure quantization module takes each residue with its 40 nearest neighbours in 3D as a local structure, embeds it with a geometric vector perceptron (GVP) encoder trained to denoise CATH structures, and assigns it to the nearest of K k-means centroids; the centroid index is the residue's structure token. A Transformer then reads the residue tokens and the structure tokens together. Its disentangled attention, adapted from DeBERTa, keeps five attention terms between residues, structure tokens and relative positions (residue-to-residue, residue-to-structure, residue-to-position, structure-to-residue and position-to-residue). The model is pretrained with structure-conditioned masked language modelling: 15% of residues are corrupted and predicted from the rest of the sequence and the uncorrupted structure tokens.
sections.source_locator: README; config.json; paper: Sections 3.1 to 3.3

sections.title: Versions and reproducibility
sections.body: The checkpoints differ in the size of the structure vocabulary K (20, 128, 512, 1024, 2048 or 4096). The paper found most metrics best at K = 2048 and made it the default. The notebook and the ProteinGym command pair ProSST-2048 with structure tokens made at vocabulary size 2048. Because the checkpoints differ in K, a result should name K and the Hugging Face revision. This page read ProSST-2048 at revision e94ffee7. The repository's ProteinGym script also needs precomputed structure tokens; the README links them on Google Drive, made from the same PDB set as ProtSSN.
sections.source_locator: README: 2 and 4.2; Hugging Face API response

facts.label: Model type
facts.value: Protein language model that takes both the amino acid sequence and the 3D structure, pretrained with a masked language model objective.
facts.source_locator: Abstract; config.json

facts.label: Architecture
facts.value: A structure quantization module (a six-layer GVP graph encoder plus a k-means codebook of K centroids) that turns a structure into discrete structure tokens, and a Transformer with sequence-structure disentangled attention. The ProSST-2048 config has 12 layers, 12 attention heads, hidden size 768, feed-forward size 3072 and relative position embeddings. The paper gives the same layers, heads and width but a feed-forward size of 3172.
facts.source_locator: config.json; paper: Section 3 and Appendix A.3

facts.label: Inputs
facts.value: An amino acid sequence plus a sequence of structure tokens. The structure tokens are computed from a PDB file by the repository's structure quantizer, with a vocabulary of 20, 128, 512, 1024, 2048 or 4096 tokens, and are shifted by 3 for special tokens before being passed to the model.
facts.source_locator: README: 2 Structure quantizer

facts.label: Outputs
facts.value: Per-position logits over residues from the masked language model head. The notebook scores a substitution as the log-probability of the mutant residue minus that of the wild type, summing over multiple substitutions. The paper also uses the representations for supervised downstream tasks.
facts.source_locator: README: 3 and 4; Abstract

steps.title: Score mutants on one protein
steps.shell:
cd zero_shot
python - <<'PY'
from transformers import AutoModelForMaskedLM, AutoTokenizer
from prosst.structure.get_sst_seq import SSTPredictor
from Bio import SeqIO
import torch
import pandas as pd
from scipy.stats import spearmanr

prosst_model = AutoModelForMaskedLM.from_pretrained("AI4Protein/ProSST-2048", trust_remote_code=True)
prosst_tokenizer = AutoTokenizer.from_pretrained("AI4Protein/ProSST-2048", trust_remote_code=True)
predictor = SSTPredictor(structure_vocab_size=2048)

residue_sequence = str(SeqIO.read('example_data/GRB2_HUMAN_Faure_2021.fasta', 'fasta').seq)
structure_sequence = predictor.predict_from_pdb("example_data/GRB2_HUMAN_Faure_2021.pdb")[0]['2048_sst_seq']
structure_sequence_offset = [i + 3 for i in structure_sequence]

tokenized_res = prosst_tokenizer([residue_sequence], return_tensors='pt')
input_ids = tokenized_res['input_ids']
attention_mask = tokenized_res['attention_mask']
structure_input_ids = torch.tensor([1, *structure_sequence_offset, 2], dtype=torch.long).unsqueeze(0)

with torch.no_grad():
    outputs = prosst_model(
        input_ids=input_ids,
        attention_mask=attention_mask,
        ss_input_ids=structure_input_ids
    )
logits = torch.log_softmax(outputs.logits[:, 1:-1], dim=-1).squeeze()

df = pd.read_csv("example_data/GRB2_HUMAN_Faure_2021.csv")
mutants = df['mutant'].tolist()
vocab = prosst_tokenizer.get_vocab()
pred_scores = []
for mutant in mutants:
    mutant_score = 0
    for sub_mutant in mutant.split(":"):
        wt, idx, mt = sub_mutant[0], int(sub_mutant[1:-1]) - 1, sub_mutant[-1]
        pred = logits[idx, vocab[mt]] - logits[idx, vocab[wt]]
        mutant_score += pred.item()
    pred_scores.append(mutant_score)

print(spearmanr(pred_scores, df['DMS_score']))
PY

profile.summary: TranceptEVE predicts the effect of mutations in a protein without training on any experimental measurement of that protein. It combines two kinds of model: Tranception, an autoregressive transformer trained across protein families on unaligned sequences, and family-specific models built from a multiple sequence alignment of the protein in question, namely weighted pseudocounts and a trained EVE model. The input is a wild-type sequence, an alignment of its family and a list of variants; the output is one fitness score per variant. The three parts are combined with weights that follow the depth of the alignment, so a protein with a shallow alignment leans on the transformer.
profile.summary_source_locator: Europe PMC abstract of PPR582395; score_trancepteve.py argument list; scoring_TranceptEVE_substitutions.sh

sections.title: How it works
sections.body: Three sources of evidence are combined at scoring time, not during training. The first is Tranception, an autoregressive transformer with attention heads specialised for contiguous subsequences, which scores a mutated sequence in both directions by default. The second is retrieval from the alignment: weighted pseudocounts at each position, computed with the sequence weighting procedure of Hopf et al. The third is EVE, a family-specific alignment model. In the paper, the wild-type sequence is encoded by each trained EVE model and decoded 200k times, and the averaged outputs give a fixed per-position prior over amino acids for the family; this is why only the wild type, not each variant, is scored with EVE. Each residue's log probability is a weighted average of the three terms, with weights set by the depth of the alignment: with fewer than 10 sequences the transformer is used alone, and with 10^5 or more the EVE and alignment weights rise to 0.8 and 0.5. The scoring script exposes the two coefficients as alpha (alignment pseudocounts) and beta (EVE); the paper names them the other way round, alpha for EVE and beta for the alignment. The script can also rescale the alignment and EVE log probabilities to match the temperature of the transformer, which the paper describes as temperature scaling of the EVE log probabilities.
sections.source_locator: Tranception README; score_trancepteve.py; paper: Section 2 and Appendix B.1, B.2, B.4

sections.title: What a run needs
sections.body: TranceptEVE is not a single downloadable model. A run needs a Tranception checkpoint, an alignment of the protein family, redundancy-based sequence weights for that alignment, and one or more trained EVE models for the same family. The alignments and weights for the ProteinGym proteins are published by the ProteinGym project, 5.2 GB of alignments and 200 MB of weights; the EVE models themselves are not in that list of downloads, and the scoring script takes a path to a folder holding them. The reference settings the maintainers used draw 200,000 samples for each EVE log probability and average five EVE seeds, 0 to 4.
sections.source_locator: scoring_TranceptEVE_substitutions.sh; score_trancepteve.py argument list; ProteinGym README Resources table; Tranception README

sections.title: Versions and reproducibility
sections.body: The variants are named after the Tranception checkpoint they use: TranceptEVE S, M and L, over Tranception Small, Medium and Large. The published script has all three output paths written out, with Medium left active. A result must name which of the three it used, and also the EVE models, because those are trained per family and are not part of a published checkpoint: different EVE training runs give different numbers. The probability recalibration flags and the aggregation coefficients are also part of the setting. The reference run switches recalibration of the EVE probabilities on and does not set the script's --retrieval_weights_manual flag, which is the option to choose the alignment and EVE weights by hand; the alpha and beta arguments default to 0.5. The paper sets the weights from alignment depth.

facts.label: Model type
facts.value: Zero-shot variant effect predictor: a hybrid of a family-agnostic autoregressive protein language model with family-specific alignment models, combined at scoring time.
facts.source_locator: Europe PMC abstract of PPR582395; ProteinGym README baseline table row TranceptEVE

facts.label: Architecture
facts.value: Tranception, an autoregressive transformer with specialised attention heads, plus two alignment-based components: weighted pseudocounts per position and EVE, a Bayesian variational autoencoder of the family alignment used as a fixed per-position prior. The three sets of log probabilities are combined per residue as a weighted average, with weights set by alignment depth in the paper; the script calls the alignment weight alpha and the EVE weight beta, the paper the reverse.

strengths.text: Reproducible as a benchmark baseline: the exact settings the ProteinGym maintainers ran are committed in the repository, including the EVE sample count, the five EVE seeds and the scoring window.

limitations.text: Expensive per protein. The reference run draws 200,000 samples for each EVE log probability, averages five seeds, and by default scores every sequence in both directions.

profile.summary: Tranception is an autoregressive transformer language model for protein fitness prediction, from the Marks lab and the OATML group. It scores a mutated protein sequence by how likely the model thinks that sequence is, and it can optionally blend that score with counts from an alignment of homologous sequences retrieved at inference time. It handles substitutions, multiple mutants and insertions or deletions, and it was published together with the ProteinGym benchmark.
profile.summary_source_locator: README: title, Abstract, Tranception; model card: Abstract

sections.title: How it works
sections.body: Tranception is a decoder-only transformer built on two ideas: making attention heads specialise, and reading patterns from contiguous subsequences. In each layer the attention heads are split into four groups; three of them apply depthwise convolutions with kernel sizes 3, 5 and 7 after the query, key and value projections, so each group mixes information over a different range. The published configuration uses a squared-relu activation, grouped ALiBi position embeddings and a 25-token vocabulary. The model was trained to predict the next residue on UniRef100, with half of the sequences reversed at random; the paper scores each sequence in both directions and averages the two log-likelihood ratios. At inference the model's own autoregressive log-likelihood can be combined with weighted pseudocounts computed at each alignment position, using the sequence weighting procedure of Hopf et al. with the default thresholds. The configuration file carries the retrieval weight for that blend; the paper selected 0.6. Scoring insertions and deletions with retrieval also needs Clustal Omega, because the mutated sequence has to be realigned.
sections.source_locator: README; config.json; paper: Figure 1 legend and Appendix B.4, B.5

sections.title: Versions and reproducibility
sections.body: Three checkpoints are published: Small, Medium and Large, downloadable as zip archives from the Marks lab server (about 400MB, 1.4GB and 3.1GB unzipped) and also on the Hugging Face hub. They differ in depth and width: 12 layers and width 768 (Small, 85M parameters), 24 and 1024 (Medium, 300M) and 36 and 1280 (Large, 700M), with parameter counts as the paper gives them. All three use a context of 1024 positions. A result must say which checkpoint was used and whether retrieval was on (the --inference_time_retrieval flag), and with retrieval it must also name the alignment and the weights file. This page read the Hugging Face revisions d1ef6271 (Large), 96f42978 (Medium) and 303ff126 (Small).

profile.summary: LOL-EVE (Language Of Life for Evolutionary Variant Effects) scores the effect of insertions and deletions (indels) in human gene promoters without task-specific training. It is a conditional autoregressive transformer trained on 13.6 million mammalian promoter sequences, each tagged with its gene, species and clade. A variant is scored by comparing how likely the model finds the reference and the variant promoter sequence.
profile.summary_source_locator: README: Abstract; Using Hugging Face Model. Model card: Key Features

sections.title: How it works
sections.body: LOL-EVE is a causal language model based on the CTRL architecture, with 12 transformer layers, hidden size 768 and 12 attention heads; the paper gives a feed-forward dimension of 8192. Each input starts with control codes for the gene, species and clade, followed by the promoter DNA between [SOS] and [EOS] tokens, one token per base so that indels do not shift the tokenisation; training sequences were up to 1000 base pairs. In the paper, the gene is represented by the mean-pooled ESM2 (650M) embedding of its canonical human protein, kept frozen and projected to the model width, which the authors say lets the model handle genes not seen in training; species and clade have learned embeddings. Position embeddings are absolute for the control codes and restart at the start of the DNA sequence. During training the control codes are dropped at random. To score a variant, the reference and variant sequences are each run through the model with the same control codes, the summed cross-entropy of each is computed, and the score is the variant's minus the reference's, with higher meaning more deleterious.
sections.source_locator: README; model card; config.json; paper: Section 2.2 and Table A1; paper: Section 2.2, equation (1)

sections.title: Versions and reproducibility
sections.body: One checkpoint is published, Marks-lab/LOL-EVE on Hugging Face; this page read revision 397bbb87. Its custom model code describes itself as a simplified wrapper that builds a standard CTRL language model with the configured sizes, and its comments say that in practice this would load the actual trained model. The wrapper does not refer to ESM embeddings or adaptive position embeddings. The repository's example_usage.py uses the same wrapper and only prints the shape of the output logits. The repository's own scoring script takes a local checkpoint, tokeniser, genome and embedding file instead. A result should state which route was used (the Hugging Face wrapper or the repository script), the Hugging Face revision, and the control codes given. The paper is the MLCB 2025 work; the model card links a bioRxiv preprint and says the link is to be updated.

facts.label: Model type
facts.value: Conditional autoregressive (causal) genomic language model for zero-shot promoter variant effect prediction.

facts.label: Architecture
facts.value: CTRL-based transformer: 12 layers, hidden size 768, 12 attention heads, feed-forward dimension 8192 (from the paper), vocabulary of 39,378 tokens, adaptive local position embeddings, with gene, species and clade control codes. In the paper the gene code is a frozen ESM2 protein embedding projected to the model width.
